To say that the intrinsically pure mind is called the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) is precisely to take True Suchness (tathatā) as the Buddha-nature (gotra).
Why is this? Because the Path is the cause for transcending the world; this is the Path of the Unconditioned Four Truths.
Nirvāṇa is likewise the ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā). This Middle Way principle is called wisdom (prajñā), and it is the attainment of Buddhahood.
Why is this called the lineage (*gotra*)? Because wisdom possesses the characteristic of being cultivated and brought forth, it is identical to the wisdom of the Buddha’s realm.
These are all explained as the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*) from the perspective of ultimate attainment.
The commentary states: This summarizes the preceding meaning; thus, it is established that the nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) has principle as its essence.
The practice-seed (*samudānīta-bīja*) is likewise accomplished from *tathatā*.
The commentary clarifies that the practice-seed is also *tathatā*; for indeed, without conduct that flows from *tathatā*, one cannot realize *tathatā*.

Because there is nothing that adorns the true practice, and because practice does not arise from the true [nature], these seeds of habituation (*vāsanā-bīja*) grasp that truth and thereby come into being.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Reaching the flow from the Dharma-realm," and so forth.

The commentary explains: "The perfuming of extensive learning" refers to the possession of the three types of wisdom—namely, hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-maya*, *cintā-maya*, and *bhāvanā-maya*). These three wisdoms...
Because it is only through the power of being permeated by the Truth that compassionate practice is initiated, it is said to "flow from the pure dharma-realm" and so forth;
the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* states: "One enters samādhi through the cultivation of wisdom derived from hearing, relying upon which one realizes entry."
Furthermore, regarding the passage in the *Awakening of Faith* that leads to "the one True Suchness," the commentary explains:

that the two Greats—the essence and the characteristic of True Suchness—act as the internal perfuming cause means that the untainted virtuous qualities of the Tathāgatagarbha are inherently possessed by sentient beings;
therefore, they receive internal perfuming. That the Great Function of True Suchness acts as the external perfuming condition...
This means that the conditions of the teachers—the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends—do not depart from the Truth, and thus they provide external perfuming.
Since these three great factors perfume the defiled consciousness-mind, it is said:

"Because it is conjoined with the defiled dharma of ignorance, when ignorance is exhausted, one says that the awakening-mind first arises; yet the mind has no initial phase, having long since transcended it."

Because one is free from subtle conceptualization, the mind abides eternally; this is called ultimate enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*). Therefore, it is said that they are "darkly united as non-dual," being solely *tathatā*.

Furthermore, because initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) merges with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), there is no longer any distinction between the initial and the original; it is simply ultimate enlightenment.
This explanation is given because the meaning of the "nature of the habit-seed" (*vāsanā-bīja-gotra*) is broad and pervasive; it should not be taken to refer merely to the initial stage of the path.
This constitutes the ultimate consummation.
Third, regarding the Sudden Teaching, it reaches [its conclusion] because there are no dualistic characteristics.
The commentary states: This teaching clarifies only that the profound, absolute spirit of sentient beings and all Buddhas share one and the same primordial limit (*prakṛti*).
This departure from words surely distinguishes between the natures of innate and acquired [tendencies]. All that follows below sets forth the reasons for this.
Therefore, the exposition of all dharmas concludes with the discussion of the three vehicles.
The commentary asks: "How so? and below, Mañjuśrī provides the answer, which may be understood according to the preceding pattern. The section above concludes...
The general conclusion regarding the beginning and end [of the teachings] shows that both the Sudden Teaching and these [preceding ones] belong to the Three Vehicles.
Third, concerning the One Vehicle, it is because it subsumes the provisional means.
The commentary states: Although the four preceding teachings differ in their *āgama* and provisional arrangements, if one investigates them thoroughly, they ultimately converge in ultimate fusion.
Because it penetrates the ocean of universal nature, it is said to encompass all preceding teachings, possessing them all in their entirety.

Regarding the statement that it "possesses the principal and its associates," this refers to the common teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). If it were merely the common teaching of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), the relationship between the principal and its associates would not yet be clearly elucidated.
Second, based on the Distinct Teaching (bhedavyavasthāna), up to the point where [the stage] is already accomplished.

The commentary states: Second, based on the following brief indication of the inconceivable cause and effect, the subsequent section extensively demonstrates their characteristics. Regarding the statement that "cause and effect are non-dual":

this refers to the fact that the dharmas subsumed under the causal gate and the dharmas subsumed under the resultant gate are complete without remainder; there are four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) regarding this.

The passage from "penetrating the basis and the correct" (*tong yi ji zheng*) through "the three vehicles and the mundane world are harmoniously integrated" (*san sheng shi jian rong tong yan shou*) clarifies that these dharma-gates are naturally and perfectly complete;
thus, it is said that they are "originally fulfilled" (*ben lai man zu*) and "already accomplished" (*yi cheng jiu*). This explains the ten aspects of dependent origination (*yuan qi*).
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says, "Reaching equality," which refers to this very point.
The commentary explains: This establishes that the lineage (*gotra*) is fused and identical with the *dharmadhātu*, pointing to empty space to manifest its characteristic.
If it manifests according to the gateways, other cases may be inferred accordingly.

The commentary states: "Manifesting according to the gateways" clarifies that the Great Dependent Origination (*mahā-pratītyasamutpāda*) is the unimpeded integration of both the circular and the sequential aspects;
because it is sequential, the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*) are not confused, and because it is circular, within each stage one cultivates the six determinations (*ṣaḍ-niyama*).

Regarding the term "six," there are six aspects of practice: first, the essential nature of the practice is determined and firm; second, regarding that which is to be realized, it is determined that it must be realized;

third, it is certain that one can sever delusions; fourth, one is determined to have faith without doubt; fifth, one is determined to deliver sentient beings; and sixth, one is certain to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

Among these six aspects of practice, the first five are of the nature of self-perfection (*svabhāva*), while the last one is of the nature of further advancement (*viśeṣa*). Within the first five, the first four are for oneself.

Regarding the two benefits: among the latter [two], the first is the benefit of others. Among the four [aspects of] the former [benefit for oneself], the first three clarify that the essence of conduct (*caryā*) and realization (*vidyā*) is complete and perfect, while the last one clarifies that the qualities of conduct are fully endowed.
Within the second [pair], the first clarifies the essential nature of conduct and realization, while the last demonstrates that such conduct is free from faults.

Therefore, the essence—being free from faults—comprises the qualities as its cause; because these two types of beneficial conduct are perfected, the fruit of Buddhahood is achieved. Thus, it is said: "and this very same [fruit]."
The Dharma is termed the "characteristic of the fruit.

Commentary on the Meaning of the *Huayan Yicheng Fenqizhang* (The Chapter on the Distinctions of the One Vehicle of the Avataṃsaka), Scroll Four Commentary on the Meaning of the *Huayan Yicheng Fenqizhang*, Scroll Five Composed by the Śramaṇa Daoting of Xi溪 Pujing Monastery [Scroll Five begins] **Section: The Distinction Between the Provisional and the Real** Now, we shall explain the distinction between the provisional and the real. Regarding this, there are two aspects: first, the general explanation; second, the specific analysis. First, the general explanation: The provisional and the real are established based on the principle of the capacity and incapacity of sentient beings to receive the teaching. That which accords with the capacity is called "real," while that which does not accord with the capacity is termed "provisional. Furthermore, the provisional and the real are distinguished according to the depth or shallowness of the principle revealed.

That which reveals the ultimate principle is called "real," while that which reveals only a partial or inferior principle is termed "provisional. Moreover, the provisional and the real are distinguished according to the breadth or narrowness of the practice encompassed. That which encompasses the vast and perfect practice is called "real," while that which encompasses only a limited or inferior practice is termed "provisional. Second, the specific analysis: Within the teachings of the Buddha, there are three vehicles and one vehicle. The three vehicles are the provisional, and the one vehicle is the real. Furthermore, within the one vehicle, there are two aspects: the common and the uncommon. The common one vehicle is the provisional, and the uncommon one vehicle is the real. Also, within the uncommon one vehicle, there are two aspects: the gradual and the sudden. The gradual is the provisional, and the sudden is the real. Moreover, within the sudden teaching, there are two aspects: the teaching of the fruit and the teaching of the cause. The teaching of the fruit is the provisional, and the teaching of the cause is the real. Furthermore, within the teaching of the cause, there are two aspects: the teaching of the principle and the teaching of the practice. The teaching of the principle is the provisional, and the teaching of the practice is the real. Finally, within the teaching of the practice, there are two aspects: the teaching of the universal and the teaching of the particular. The teaching of the universal is the provisional, and the teaching of the particular is the real. Thus, from the perspective of the capacity of beings, the teaching of the three vehicles is provisional and the one vehicle is real; from the perspective of the depth of principle, the common one vehicle is provisional and the uncommon one vehicle is real; from the perspective of the method of entry, the gradual is provisional and the sudden is real; from the perspective of the stage of attainment, the teaching of the fruit is provisional and the teaching of the cause is real; from the perspective of the content of the teaching, the teaching of the principle is provisional and the teaching of the practice is real; and from the perspective of the scope of application, the teaching of the universal is provisional and the teaching of the particular is real. It should be understood that these distinctions are all established for the purpose of guiding sentient beings toward the ultimate truth. [End of Scroll Five]

Because the Buddha does not transcend the stages [of practice], he provisionally conforms to them in order to attract those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Why is this?

Regarding the meaning of the twelve stages (*dvādaśa-vihāra*), which combines the ten stages—such as the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*)—with the preceding [two], the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

1. **The Stage of the Spiritual Lineage** (*gotra-vihāra*): This refers to the Bodhisattva whose nature is inherently virtuous and whose nature is naturally endowed with the qualities of a Bodhisattva, sustaining the seeds of all Buddha-dharmas.
2. **The Stage of Practice through Resolute Conviction** (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*): This refers to the period from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*).

The fourth is the higher training in ethics (*adhiśīla*), the fifth is the higher training in mind (*adhicitta*), and the sixth, seventh, and eighth are called the higher training in wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), which is divided into three types: namely, the stage of higher wisdom associated with the six factors of enlightenment (*ṣaḍ-bodhyaṅga-saṃprayukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra*);

Second, regarding those who do not regress, they extend up to those of the Three Vehicles.

The commentary states: "From the Śrāvaka up to the patience regarding suffering" refers to the wisdom of the lower patience (*kṣānti*) concerning the Truth of Suffering within the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
At the moment of arising, one realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and no longer regresses.

For those who have reached the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) stage of the *pratyekabuddha*, because their faculties are somewhat sharper, they do not regress even at the final moment of their preparatory application (*prayoga*).

As for Bodhisattvas who have reached the tenth stage of the "Vow" (*daśa-praṇidhāna*), it means that once the wisdom of the preparatory application (*prayoga-jñāna*) arises with courageous vigor and pursuit, there is no regression; this should be understood as applying to the lower stages as well.
The "objection" refers to the following objection: "It is evident that the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas are distinct; why then do you discuss non-retrogression for both in the same place?
This is answered generally by the passage beginning with "One should know," and so forth.
It may also be that Bodhisattvas reach such eons as these. The commentary states:

The former was based on the Buddha-nature where those of the "Superior" stage do not regress; this refers to the three stages of the "Ordinary Persons" (*pṛthagjana*) in the *Yogācāra*, wherein all may regress.
Why is this so? It is because the former refers to superior practice, while this treatise concerns the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*); thus, each establishes its own sense of non-regression.
[The text] ends with "the ear. Within the stage of the three insights (*trividyā*), reaching this point is called the "Abiding in Practice through Resolute Conviction" (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).
The commentary states: "The Bodhisattva abiding in practice through resolute conviction" precisely clarifies the mode of cultivation practiced by those of the Three Sages (*tri-śaikṣa*).

Regarding the term "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*), it refers to the transition from the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) into this [state]. As for what the practice is and what its characteristics are, the following is shown as an answer:
at times, one who possesses the complete excellence of wisdom and is endowed with the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is able to receive and retain all phenomena.
This refers to the four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*): investigating name, object, intrinsic nature, and specific difference, which are understood to exist only as designations (*prajñapti*).

In truth, there is nothing [substantial] therein; those capable of awakening to and entering into its meaning and principle are said to possess "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūtajñāna*), because they have thoroughly and correctly known the four—namely, name and so forth—as being distinct from consciousness and as having no existence apart from consciousness.
Alternatively, this refers to the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "What are the characteristics of the sublime practices that are cultivated? Briefly, there are two kinds."
This refers to merit and wisdom. Furthermore, it is said that according to the general characteristics of the six *pāramitās*, they all pertain to both Mahāyāna paths.
The Dharma Master explains: those that are practiced together with wisdom and assist in accomplishing the activity of wisdom are all called "wisdom";
those that are practiced together with merit and assist in accomplishing the activity of merit are all called "merit. This...

Regarding the establishment of its essential nature through its associated factors and general characteristics, since it takes the six pāramitās as its substance, the characteristics of these six perfections are not presented separately herein. At times, it may not be thus, for it is not fixed;
at times, it is characterized by complete mindfulness and concentration; and at times, it becomes deluded.
It may appear as if it were not giving, yet it gives by truly inducing [the recipient] to a lower state;
or at times, it may seem to discard [the gift], yet this is wisdom rather than a lack of wisdom; or at one time, regarding what appears to be great diligence, it is actually not diligence;
or due to internal intention, it is wisdom; or at one time, upon hearing a teaching, it may appear as if there is no patience, yet it is indeed patience.
Furthermore, because there are five fears and other such categories, these collectively summarize the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s six pāramitās;

that they all possess the characteristic of advancing and retreating is stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun) as follows: "In this stage, one has not yet realized the true suchness (*tathatā*) of consciousness-only;
although one cultivates various superior practices through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), the power of śamatha and vipaśyanā is still weak."
The commentary says: "This refers to all [stages] up to that point, as explained there.
The explanation states: this points to the middle stage by analogy with the first and the last. For example, when higher stages are compared to those below, they are superior;
when compared to those above, they are inferior. Why is this? Because the evidence for comparison differs.
If one relies on the Final Teaching (Jiǒngjiào), it is spoken of in terms of the stages of seeing (dṛṣṭamārga) and cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

The commentary states: Because this teaching is mature, it does not resemble the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna); rather, it directly clarifies the distinctions among the ten stages (daśabhūmi) of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, it does not differentiate between the paths of seeing and cultivation as separate entities.
Furthermore, because one has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression prior to the [first] ground.

The commentary explains: "Furthermore, regarding the distinctions within the stages of the lower practices, the three ranks of the *śaikṣas* (the Three Worthies) are termed 'positions' because they are adjacent to the ultimate and subordinate to the sages;

the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are termed 'practices' (*caryā*) because there are four reasons why they do not enter the [definitive] stages: first, because progress and retreat are not fixed; second..."

1) Because the ten minds of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) lack fixed stages; 2) because the three [levels] have not yet followed the Dharma-realm in practicing the vast conduct; 3) because they have not yet attained the Dharma-body to manifest the Buddha-lineage (*gotra*).
