This teaching is designated according to its stage; because it distinguishes the specific stages of practice, it belongs solely to the category of "practice" (*caryā*).
As stated extensively in the *Mūlamahāyānasaṃgraha-sūtra* (or *Bunyō-kyō*), it is as explained therein.

The commentary states: "Before determining whether [the stages] are higher or lower, one first establishes that they are not [fixed] stages. Why? Because they consist merely of the ten minds mixed with cultivation."
Furthermore, it says that the following section clarifies the characteristics of faith (*śraddhā-lakṣaṇa*).

It states that those who have gradually progressed from the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) and encountered Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to resolve upon *bodhicitta* are precisely what are called "Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths" (*daśa-śraddhā-caryā-pratipanna*) in their practice.

This passage below demonstrates their specific characteristics: "faith-conception" (*śraddhā-saṃjñā*) refers to the longing desire for contemplative visualization (*bhāvanā*), yet at this stage, the objective referent (*ālambana*) has not yet been attained.
Because it is realized, it is next stated that they are also called "provisional names" (*prajñapti*) and so forth. This refers to faith, diligence, and so on;

by the phrase "and so on," one further includes mindfulness, concentration of mind, wisdom of mind, the mind of giving, the mind of precepts, the mind of protection, the mind of aspiration, and the mind of dedication.
These constitute the bodhisattva’s ability to transform sentient beings even slightly, having already surpassed all the wholesome stages (*kuśala-bhūmi*) of the two vehicles and all other [stages].
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas nurture ten mental states as the "sacred embryo" (āryagarbha).

These ten mental states serve as the causes for the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) within the nature of the cultivated seeds (*śikṣamāṇagotra*); they are added here because the cause differs from the fruit.
Furthermore, does the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* extend even to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)?

The commentary states: regarding the "patience through practice" (*śikṣā-kṣānti*) mentioned in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, that scripture explains that from the patience through practice up to the Vajra-peak (*vajra-mūrdhan*), all constitute the thirteen Dharma-teachers (*dharma-bhāṇaka*).
The textual citations and explanations for establishing these are extensive and detailed; herein, we shall briefly describe the characteristics of this patience.

Having immediately resolved upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta and constantly cultivating the contemplation that all things within the three realms are impure in every moment, one attains the gate of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-kṣānti*).
Abiding in the family of the Buddhas and practicing the six points of respectful harmony, there is no regression.

However, those who practice the ten wholesome paths prior to this patience are at the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*); because they have not yet attained what is realized, they are subject to regression. That is to say:
Because one advances when encountering superior conditions and retreats when encountering inferior conditions, it is likened to being carried east or west by the wind.

One should know that within this stage, they have not yet entered the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; upon entering the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they will attain the stage of non-retrogression, which corresponds to the initial practice of patience (*kṣānti*).
This is to be understood accordingly.
"Even according to the *Sūtra on Original Karma*, one does not fall back until [the sixth stage] is attained.
The commentary explains: "Even according to the *Sūtra on Original Karma*" and below serves to address and resolve an objection. That is to say, there is an objection:

"In the *Sūtra on Original Karma*, the sixth stage, the Abode of Right Mindfulness (*samyak-citta-vihāra*), still admits of falling back; why then do you say above that from the very beginning of the ten abodes one does not fall back?"
The claim that one falls back is based on the Sūtras; however, when raising doubts regarding the development of faith, the Śāstra explains it away as follows:

"It is manifested as a regression in order to rouse the minds of those who are lax and negligent. If one considers the actual reality, however, one attains non-regression immediately upon the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
As for its characteristics, they are as extensively explained in that [text].
The commentary states: This refers to the characteristics of the mind-generation of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*).

Because one destroys ignorance and partially realizes the *dharmatā* within this initial stage, it is said that "one partially attains the vision of the *dharmakāya*" and is able to manifest the eight aspects of enlightenment throughout the ten directions.

The Way manifests its transformative function arising from its essence; furthermore, those who assume a body through the power of vows manifest a superior body by means of the three great vows of mind, which differs from ordinary, ignorant beings who receive various bodies bound by the constraints of karma.
Moreover, regarding those at the stage of samādhi who obtain a partial vision of the Reward Body Buddha (saṃbhogakāya), it is said that they have not yet attained [the ultimate] for themselves.
For this reason, when the mind is concentrated in goodness, one beholds the sublime marks; when the mind is distracted, one sees only the physical body.

Therefore, these differ from the constant enjoyment of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) experienced by those dwelling on the stages (bhūmi), which is seen only upon encountering it. As for the lower practices they cultivate, one may know that they accord with the nature of giving (dāna).
Furthermore, according to the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty, one should know that [the subsequent stages] double in number from the preceding.
The commentary states: "The ten levels of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) are called 'sages' (*ārya*) because they are Bodhisattvas; 'understanding' constitutes their essence.

They are called 'sages' because they are correct, for they are in profound accord with the true principle (*tattva*). Moreover, because they have attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) true Dharma within their minds, they are called sages."

From this, it is also proven that this stage of the Bodhisattva possesses partial realization; those ten stages of faith are designated as "ordinary" and must certainly be understood as being comprised of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Therefore, one should know that the distinctions [of the stages] become manifest upon reaching this point.

The commentary states: Comparing the stage prior to the teaching herein with the stage prior to the initial teaching, the difference in their excellence is as vast as the distance between heaven and earth.
Question: Does this teaching not reach the point where it no longer resembles that [initial teaching]?

The commentary states: Regarding the initial question and the two subsequent answers, the reference within the answers to the "two vehicles" (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) as being likewise "matured" and so forth means that those of fixed nature in the two vehicles and those of no-nature (icchantikas) will all attain Buddhahood.
Since they all attain Buddhahood, there is no differentiation of stages or ranks;
rather, each is made to realize it. Therefore, this is not like the former case.
"If one relies on the Sudden Teaching, [to say] 'it is' is itself a perversion.
The commentary explains: "If one relies on the following, it refers to the teaching that employs 'dispelling' and 'brushing away' to eliminate marks.
The phrase "in a single thought" below indicates the realization and entry; "if one sees" below criticizes emotional views, decisively showing that one must not establish fixed positions.
"If one expresses [the ultimate] by means of provisional words" refers to such cases as these.

The commentary explains: "To express by means of provisional words" means to rely upon words that lack sequential order to reveal that teaching which is free from characteristics and transcends all gradations;
thus, it cites the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, saying: "The first stage is itself the eighth stage. This statement is brief.
Because it was not yet complete, the fourth long passage of that sutra states: "O Mahamati, regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there is no sequential continuity;
it is taught as the non-existence of all conceptual proliferation (vikalpa) and the dharma of quiescence. Within the verses, there are seven stanzas;
the final two stanzas clarify that the stages (bhūmi) are not established, stating: "The tenth stage is the first; the first is the eighth stage; the ninth is..."
The seventh and seventh (49) also become eight; the second becomes the third, the fourth becomes the fifth, and the fifth becomes the sixth.

Since there is nothing that exists, what sequence can there be? The commentary explains: the first seven phrases correspond in meaning to the final phrase, which, according to principle, is entirely extinguished.
That the Ten Stages constitute the beginning is because they equally realize Suchness; that the beginning constitutes [the end] is...
Regarding the eighth stage: the first stage is not moved by afflictions and is thus identical to the immovable [eighth stage]. Regarding the ninth being the seventh:
the ninth is identical to the seventh, the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Regarding the seventh also being the eighth:

the pure contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*) is identical to the eighth. Regarding the second being the third: it is identical to the patience of faith (*adhimukti-kṣānti*). Regarding the fourth...
The fifth is identical to *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformative patience). Regarding the fifth being the sixth:

the attainment of the light of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*) in the fifth stage (*bhūmi*) and the acquisition of supreme *prajñā* in the sixth stage share the same meaning as "wisdom" (*jñāna*).

As for "nothing exists," what is the sequence? This refers to the preceding scriptural passage; while in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) there is no characteristic of sequential continuity, in this present text—

The first phrase briefly cites the essential point of the single line within the section on "Conciseness through Identical Meaning"; the second phrase, however, relies on the principle that all things are utterly extinguished and nothing can be pointed out through words.
Thus, one should not mistake this for the existence of a fixed state. The text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samantabhadrotsāhana-parivarta* (Sishiyi) is explicit and easy to understand.
If one relies on the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) to reach this stage of skillful means (*upāya*), the commentary states:
First, based on the teachings, the meanings are opened up; these are categorized and explained in the following list.

This means that the stages and practices elucidated by the preceding four teachings—whether great or small, gradual or sudden—are all *āgama* (scriptural transmissions) bestowed according to the capacities of sentient beings.
If it is argued that these are all preliminary signs for this teaching, they are nonetheless subsumed within this [present] stage simultaneously.
Second, according to the distinct teachings, because [the stages] are reached and because they are perfectly interfused (yuanrong).

The commentary states: The first [point] establishes the positions based on the teachings; that is to say, from the beginning down to the formal naming, they are designated as "sequential and interfused" (xingbu yuanrong), because they are sequential.

Regarding the phrase "the six stages are different," as for what are called the six stages: if one opens up the ten faiths (*śraddhā*) from the preceding [stage] and combines the equal enlightenment (*samabodhi*) with the following, or if one opens up the equal enlightenment from the following and combines the ten faiths with the preceding, these are all the six stages.
Because they are perfectly interfused (*pariniṣpanna-yoga*), by attaining any single stage, one attains all stages.
As for the question "Why is this so?", it probes the characteristic of perfect interfusion; the subsequent section provides the explanation based on the meaning to clarify this point.

Each "old" character (gu-zì) constitutes a distinct meaning: first, the meaning of the six aspects; second, the meaning of the primary and its associates (*zhǔ-bàn*), which is the ten profound mysteries (*shí xuán-yì*);
third, mutual identity (*xiāng-jí*) based on essence; fourth, mutual inclusion (*xiāng-rù*) based on function; and fifth, perfect interfusion (*yuán-róng*) based on the Dharma-realm (*fǎ-jìe*).
Because these are all fundamentally characterized by pervasive interpenetration, each stage is clearly distinct yet mutually inclusive.
The Scripture says, "Abiding in the ultimate," which refers to this very meaning.
The commentary explains: based on the scripture to demonstrate the meaning, first there is the reliance on the scripture; therefore, what follows demonstrates the meaning.

Furthermore, the subsequent section clarifies the mutual penetration of cause and effect within each and every stage (*avasthā*), manifesting their pervasive interconnection and sovereign freedom; thus, by means of the cause—
If taken from the perspective of causes, they are all bodhisattvas; if taken from the perspective of fruits, they are all Buddhas.
Thus, purity and mixture are unimpeded, and the hidden and the manifest are perfected simultaneously.
Second, the clarification of stages according to retribution is explained in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (Xingqi-pin).
The commentary states: Because phenomena manifest in accordance with past causes, it is said that "the stages and characteristics are clarified by way of retribution.
This refers to the specific enumeration and explanation of the characteristics. That is to say, regarding the inexhaustible dharma-gates, they are established as the vajra-seed by way of the Dharma;

the analogy is as explained in the *Xingqi-pin* (Chapter on the Arising of Nature), which says: "It is like a person who eats a small amount of vajra; it will never be digested, nor will it [be lost]."

Just as one who dwells together with the physical body must pass through that body until reaching the adamantine limit (*vajra-koṭi*)—the Tathāgata’s perfect and inexhaustible Dharma-gate is likewise so.

If there are those who see or hear [this teaching], they must not dwell together with afflictions (*kleśa*), but must pass through delusive phenomena (*mṛṣā-dharma*) until reaching the limit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is precisely the stage of seeing and hearing.
The second point, "attaining the stage of practice through understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), also refers to this same meaning.

The commentary explains: "Attaining the stage of practice through understanding" means that because the seeds of past causes were superior, one now produces understanding and accomplishes practice in this life.
This refers to the person descending from Tuṣita to manifest signs; "one who has emerged from the evil realms" refers to this son of heaven.

At that time, although he heard the Dharma, because his practice of the precepts was lax, he fell into the Avīci Hell; yet because his momentum toward the Mahāyāna was swift, he emerged from the evil realm and was born in Tuṣita Heaven.
There, the celestial drum sounded, prompting him to immediately repent and leap directly to the tenth stage.

Therefore it is said that he "immediately attained the Vimala-samādhi" and so forth; this is precisely the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) within the stages, as explained in the "Chapter on Minor Characteristics."

This is the same as the explanation of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) in the Tang translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "As when Sudhana first [enters] the ten stages of faith" refers to the characteristics of practicing by way of assigned stages.
Regarding the phrase "in one lifetime, in one body," it means that this is the final spiritual friend at the ultimate end of the causal stage;
thus, Qingliang said: "Entering the profound gate of Samantabhadra, there is never any separate essence."
"Third, regarding the stage of realizing the ocean of fruition, it says 'one shall see me when [the time] arrives.

The commentary explains: 'Realization and entry' refers to birth. This means that, as shown below by way of persons, these are the friends through whom Sudhana gathers virtues and accomplishes the causes;
since they have gathered the virtues of the preceding stages to form a single cause, they thereby manifest the abiding of the fruition."
Because it refers to the subsequent stage, it says, "I shall attain perfect enlightenment in the future. One should know that what follows explains this according to its meaning;

as can be inferred from the preceding, although the subsequent stage belongs to the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*), it is explained here in contrast to the causal stage, and thus it is entirely subsumed within the stage of retribution (*vipāka*).
"Third, clarifying the stages by way of practice, extending up to the ocean of worlds.
The commentary states: This correctly elucidates the supreme characteristics to manifest the function of wisdom.

That is to say, "one's own stage" refers to the specific position one currently occupies, while "superior progress" refers to advancing toward subsequent heights and depths. In this section, the reference to "the person and their body" means that it is based upon...
When it is said that both the primary and secondary retributions are fully manifested, this indicates that the characteristics of the world-nature (*jagat-prakṛti*) are most abundantly displayed;

when it is said that the primary retribution is manifested in its stages, this shows that the karmic fortune of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) is no small matter—both serve to manifest his excellence.
That he attains universal vision demonstrates that the function of his wisdom is inexhaustible.
If it is so for the fleshly eyes of those in the three vehicles, it is likewise for all others.

The commentary states that this cites the inferior to reveal the superior. "If [it is so] for the three vehicles" below cites the inferior; furthermore, "and as for those [others]" below reveals the superior.
To say that the fleshly eye sees only matters within the trichiliocosm refers to the fleshly eye as discussed in the systems of the three vehicles.
Because the eye sees only forms within its own range, the ancient masters said: "The fleshly eye is obstructed and not pervasive. If one were to see what is below, this would be a counter-argument.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "it can [function] in a single thought-moment," this indicates that the inconceivable application of wisdom gathers sentient beings and brings about great benefit;
therefore, all [stages] reach up to, but do not exceed, the *vimalā* (Stainless) concentration. If this is true for a single thought-moment, it is likewise for subsequent moments.
Because all are thus, it is said that "moment by moment" [this practice] benefits sentient beings without end; only then does one see the conduct of Samantabhadra.
As for the phrase "its portion of merit reaches the gate of causes," the commentary explains:

since the preceding wisdoms are both merit and knowledge, these two feet are manifested together; therefore, concentration (*samādhi*) is taken as the essence of merit, and thus all virtues [are established].
The statement that "a single *caṅku* of glass is manifested" means that because this Bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom are fully perfected, the one inherently contains the many.

Just as that glass is a clear mirror that reflects both the distant and the near simultaneously, so too within the "returning to the source," there occurs the manifestation of the *caṅku* of glass and other such matters.
One should know that what follows clarifies the stages of attainment by way of the causal gate.
The term "hence" (gu) serves to distinguish that the stage of the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*) is indeed inexpressible and cannot be demonstrated.
If one refers to the fulfillment of faith and so forth, up to the detailed explanation, the commentary states:
"If one refers to the attainment of the stage after the fulfillment of faith," this means that once practice is perfected, one enters the stage; [this is] what has arisen.
"Activity and function pervade the entire Dharma-realm" means that by realizing one thing, all things are realized; thus, activity and function are without fixed direction.

As the sutra shows below regarding the "portion of merit," it further clarifies "essence and function": not being separate from [the essence] is its essence, while the ability to manifest [phenomena] and so forth is its function.
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of subtle signs such as the eight marks mentioned below, this has already been seen in the preceding text.
One should reflect upon all of this.
Therefore, it should be understood that this leads to such a teaching.
The commentary states: "Ultimately" serves as a distinction. The phrase "therefore, it should be understood" refers back to the stages and positions of practice of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
"Contrasting with those of the three vehicles" refers to the provisional selection and manifestation [of the One Vehicle]. As for "Why is this so?", it interrogates their differences;

by explaining that they are vastly distinct from the perspective of the three vehicles below, it shows that there are such distinctions in the establishment of the doctrinal forms (*śāstra-lakṣaṇa*) according to the capacities of beings for the sake of gathering and transforming them.
However, if one investigates the ultimate realization, it resides solely in the One Vehicle, which is perfectly interfused and endowed with all virtues. Therefore, Qingliang said:

In the causal stages of the first four teachings, there is [the presence of] the ultimate fruit, whereas in this [teaching], that meaning is entirely absent; students must not fail to reflect upon this.
Question: How does the "ultimate" (zhi) in the aforementioned Final Teaching differ from this?
The commentary states: Since [the factors] arise in the same position, one may raise an objection by following the conclusion; please attempt to state it.
The answer is: because that [position] extends to all six positions.

The commentary states: Their stages are identical, yet their functions differ. Therefore, although in the stage of non-retrogression within the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-yāna), one attains samādhi and becomes mystically unified with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the eightfold manifestation of Buddhahood is displayed through the arising of function based on realization;

because this is manifested only partially, one has not yet attained mastery in the subsequent stages. Regarding the statement "because it has not been attained," it means that if one were to grant it [to them], it would be appropriate.

If one were to take away [the teaching] by means of the division of the *śāsana* (teaching), it would be because it is established in the *Āgamas*; therefore, it is said that "one has not yet attained" and that it is merely a temporary transformation.
This, however, is not so. Below, it clarifies that in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), one realization is all realizations;
thus, they arise simultaneously, for all are attained. As for the statement "in reality, the initial awakening is true practice": is this the actual practice? First.
The *śāstrakāra* [states] that there are six stages.
Question: Since the meanings are already different, does this function arise [only] at this point?

Explanation: This refers back to the distinction between the final perfection [of the previous stage] and the subsequent doubt regarding the simultaneous fulfillment of faith and the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) within the stage of practice.
[The question] asks:
Why is this said? [The answer] is: It is for the sake of providing a skillful means to reach [the ultimate goal] that this was first stated.

The commentary explains: It is truly because the Way of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is so lofty it cannot be looked up to and so profound it cannot be fathomed that it is entrusted to that [other teaching].

This statement is made because [the practitioner] rides upon the functioning of the same stage to inspire faith and submission, so that they may subsequently proceed to the Higher Vehicle (*uttarayāna*).
Question: Since one has already reached the subsequent stages from this single stage, why is it necessary to speak further?

Explanation: This refers back to the doubt regarding the perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) mentioned above; since there is also the sequential progression (*xingbu*), it is therefore necessary to explain it again.
The answer states that this applies to all subsequent stages, from the first to the last.

The commentary explains: "Successive progression" (*xingbu*) refers to the provisional designation of the teachings (*jiaoxiang shishe*), while "perfect interfusion" (*yuanrong*) refers to the essential nature, qualities, and functions (*lixing deyong*).

This means that successive progression does not obstruct perfect interfusion; thus, within each preceding stage, all stages are present, and perfect interfusion does not obstruct successive progression.
Therefore, it is said that the subsequent stages are themselves the entirety of the initial stage; this is like using the initial stage as a precedent for the subsequent ones.

The meaning is that since the initial stage already possesses the subsequent stages, and the subsequent stages likewise possess the initial stage, it is only through this mutual inclusion of the prior and the posterior that the characteristics of the harmoniously integrated stages are revealed.
Question: If one possesses the latter from the very beginning, does that mean one cannot obtain the former?

Explanation: If one possesses the latter from the beginning, it is also possible to question whether one can obtain the former. Since the latter possessing the former is not [admitted], by analogy, one questions whether the former and latter can both be obtained.
If they can be obtained, then both the former and latter are obtained; if they cannot be obtained, then neither the latter nor the former is obtained. Why is this so?
For this reason, the beginning and the end are not mutually separated.
The answer states: "It is indeed so; however, because one has reached [the end], the beginning cannot be attained.

The commentary explains: Since the initial seal permits the phrasing of the question, it says "it is indeed so"; however, from "but" onwards, it answers that the end is already present within the beginning.
Therefore, the answer below fully incorporates the initial [explanation].
Question: If this is so, why does the sequence of descending to the steps follow a specific order?
Explanation: Because the preceding and succeeding [stages] mutually incorporate one another, it is difficult to distinguish the order of descent; hence, this question arises.
Answer: This is because it does not contradict this sutra.
The commentary states: First, there is a general heading; second, there is a specific enumeration below.

As for the statement that "the various stages are established through the mutual fusion and non-obstruction [of the two]," this is explained according to the gate of causes and dependent origination; therefore, it differs from the provisional establishments set forth in other teachings.

First, regarding "establishing the ear by conforming to the gates": this means that by conforming to the characteristics of their distinct meanings, they do not contradict the various teachings of those gates;
therefore, it is said that they "provisionally accord with the Three Vehicles," and so forth. Second, regarding "conforming to the essence by way of the dharma":

this means that by conforming to its actual substance, the real virtues of the fundamental dharma are fully manifested; therefore, it is said that "the preceding and succeeding penetrate one another," which constitutes the distinction.
This is the teaching; it is like the "distinctive characteristics" (lakṣaṇa), but one should understand that what follows reveals its comprehensive inclusion and harmonious integration.
Question: If this is so, does it refer to the initial [stage] up to the perfected mind (*paripūrṇa-citta*)?

Explanation: This refers back to the preceding [point] while anticipating the subsequent difficulty regarding the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā*). The meaning is that if the initial [stage] were to possess the subsequent [stages], it would necessarily be the initial [stage].
Question: For what reason is it discussed that the mind is only fully complete at the tenth stage? Answer:
Because, according to the distinct teachings of the individual vehicles, one merely practices [the stages] up to that point.
Commentary: This answer is given by relying on the provisional positions of the original vehicle; thus, in the original vehicle, one attains perfect enlightenment from the very first thought-moment.
When one contemplates that all [stages] are established as provisional stations (*kaji*), then the ten stages of faith (*jūshin*) constitute the stage of entry (*nyūi*).

Although they are provisionally designated as those [subsequent] stages, their actual accomplishment is sudden; therefore, it is said that "all these positions are attained at once. Since these positions are identical to those [subsequent] stages, the name "attaining a stage" is applied only from the perspective of the perfected mind (*man-shin*).
Question: If that is so, one should ask: to what extent must one go to be called "perfected in faith" (*śraddhā-paripūrṇa*)?
Explanation: This refers to the meaning of "Buddha" as established by attaining the stage of entry (*avatāra-bhūmi*) mentioned previously.
Answer: It is through faith that one reaches completion; other points should be understood by analogy.

The commentary states: Although one has ascended to the first stage, because this achievement is due to the perfection of practice, it is designated merely as "the fulfillment of faith" based on its functional capacity.
The period of cultivation for the fourth [stage] extends to three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

The commentary states: The preceding section has established the accomplishment of merit through the successive stages (*bhūmi*), and since these stages necessarily involve time, this section follows.

If we proceed according to the subsequent analysis of the three faculties (*indriya*) based on the teachings, the "lower" refers to those who are slow, while for the "upper" faculty, it is said that they require only three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

This means that one who plants the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) within a single lifetime is at the stage of the "provisioning path" (*sambhāra-mārga*) of the Hīnayāna; "liberation" here refers to the portion of *nirvāṇa*.
This is because one plants the causes at that time. "Conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) refers to the stage of preparatory application;
"penetration" (*nirveda*) is the wisdom-factor of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is also a cause, for at this time one applies effort and practice to enter into it accordingly.
Third, "attaining the fruit of the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣayaphala*) refers to the ultimate state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This is the timing of their maturation; if there is any delay, it occurs within sixty minor kalpas because those of middling faculties who are Pratyekabuddhas have sharp faculties and are thus enlightened.

As for those of superior faculties who become Buddhas, they must pass through four births and a hundred kalpas, completing an incalculable aeon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), before their supreme excellence finally manifests.
In this context, the number of kalpas reaches three asaṃkhyeyas.
The commentary explains that the quantity of the aforementioned kalpas is indicated by taking one kalpa of water, fire, and so forth as a single unit;
this refers to the eighty small kalpas (antarakalpas) of increase and decrease within the ten prior destruction kalpas (saṃvartakalpas).
Since nine kalpas destroy sentient beings and one kalpa destroys the receptacle world, the Chapter on Kalpas states: "Nineteen [kalpas] involve the destruction of sentient beings from the majority;
twenty-one kalpas concern only the receptacle world. At that time, the great earth blazes everywhere, and the three thousandfold world-system becomes a mass of fierce fire.
Within this, the original number is eighty, and at the end of the cycles of increase and decrease, there is water.
After a fire disaster, the number increases tenfold each time until it reaches one thousand sixty, which constitutes one asaṃkhyeya; the remaining two follow this same pattern.
Therefore, it is said that the three asaṃkhyeyas are calculated based on this.
Question: Why is it that those of inferior faculties take so much time?

Explanation: Because the inferior [faculties] are restricted to three births while the superior [faculties] pass through immeasurable [eons], these two are utterly contradictory; therefore, this section is established.
Answer: Because it can endure for a long time, it is called "much.
The commentary states: Only when the faculties are superior and the duration is extended can the practice that is difficult to perform be manifested.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the remainder is as explained therein.

The commentary states: First, two interpretations are presented. Within these, the phrase "precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth" further includes liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
that is, it refers to the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*). Because one must pass through kalpas of time to realize this body, the four periods are enumerated.
*Asaṃkhyeya* means "immeasurable kalpas," where *kalpa* signifies a period of time. As for the "four outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) perfections":

1. "Defilements" (*āsrava*) refers to the meaning of loss and deficiency; [this teaching] cannot practice the six perfections simultaneously because it reveals this doctrine to be inferior—the four *pāramitās* being the first four of the six.
2. Regarding the cultivation of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over a hundred eons:

this teaching emphasizes the cultivation of the merit-portion (*puṇya-bhāga*). 3. Regarding the arduous cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) after leaving the household life: [this refers to] the sixth [perfection].
The latter one after the crossing is also a portion of wisdom; the cultivation of the remaining [factors] may be inferred accordingly.
If based on the Initial Teaching (śāstra), it takes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* according to the Sūtras.
The commentary states: although the duration of time is fixed at three *kalpas* for both, being equally small in scope, their quantities differ in terms of extension and brevity.
It is shown by saying:
"However, these kalpas reach up to three asaṃkhyeyas.

The commentary explains: First, there is a selection; second, an inquiry; third, a summary; and finally, the indication of characteristics. This refers to the great kalpas (mahākalpa) of water, fire, and so forth.
Because this further equates [the kalpa] with the three calamities of wind, it is discussed in terms of their repetition; therefore, it is called "great. Thus, the Chapter on Kalpas states:

"It is produced first and abandoned last. One should know that the sun, moon, years, and small kalpas (antarakalpa) encompass the two types of increase and decrease [of the life-span], while the four, six, and middle [kalpas] are subsumed under the name of a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
Taking these as the measure, the calamities of water, fire, and wind proceed in succession, with seven calamities of fire occurring first.
After one water disaster and seven water disasters, there occurs one wind disaster. The first two *dhyānas* are destroyed by the wind;
fire can destroy the third *dhyāna*, but nothing can destroy the fourth *dhyāna*.
Because water, fire, and wind disasters cannot reach the measure of a *asaṃkhyeya*, this constitutes the three *asaṃkhyeyas* of great kalpas at which a Bodhisattva is about to ascend.
At the time of his perfect enlightenment, he took hundreds of thousands of kalpas of water and fire as the base number, multiplying them successively by two until they reached the incalculable;
this is clearly evident from the text.
Furthermore, within this teaching, it refers to reaching the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The commentary explains that this is based on the Buddha’s clarification of kalpas to manifest the timing of encountering the Sage and advancing in cultivation; it is not restricted by the numerical count of water or fire [kalpas].
Furthermore, according to the *Mūla-karma-sūtra*, one attains Buddhahood after reaching one kalpa.

The commentary states that this refers to the cultivation of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over a hundred kalpas; because it is said that in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) the cultivation of merit and wisdom is partial, it is therefore described as being merely a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
As for "with a single verse," the verse says: "Heaven and earth, this world, and the Hall of Much Learning (*Prasannatā-śālā*)."

In the Brahma palaces and celestial realms throughout the ten directions, there was no Great Śramaṇa who was a Bull-King among men; having searched the earth, mountains, and forests, he found none his equal.
Because he recited this single verse with such diligent application, he surpassed Maitreya by nine kalpas and attained realization first.
Question: Does the statement regarding the three incalculable eons refer to the attainment of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body)?
Explanation: This question is raised because there may be doubt as to whether the physical body contradicts the realization of ultimate truth; therefore, this inquiry is extended. Answer:
It is from the perspective of this Initial Teaching (*śāstric* or *pāramitāyāna*) that such a statement is made.
The commentary states: It takes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of refined practice to achieve the *nirmāṇakāya*. There are four reasons for this, as each "therefore" (*hi*) represents one reason.
If one follows the Ultimate Teaching (*paryantavāda*), it is not discussed in terms of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The commentary states: “The manifestation of the ritual marks refers to the reality [of the fruit], while the response is profound and distinct; this is not the provisional teaching that explains according to the characteristics of transformation.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: “until incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas. The commentary states:
“This is to establish the meaning of the ultimate reality; thus, the duration of the kalpas is difficult to measure, as the meaning contains the sense of indeterminacy.”
Furthermore, a sutra states: "It is because I have reached ultimate discernment. The commentary explains:

This was manifested as a provisional expedient (upāya) by resorting to the bestowal of a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa); however, this is not the case here. Therefore, it was stated above that [the Buddha spoke] "throughout immeasurable kalpas" in the sutra.
Furthermore, even after a hundred kalpas, it remains a transformation (*nirmāṇa*).

The commentary explains that this distinguishes [the Buddha] from those of provisional capacity and the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). First, there is the distinction; second, the inquiry; third, the explanation. Within the explanation, by means of "the Lesser" and what follows, it clarifies the partiality of the practices of the Lesser Vehicle;
and by citing the "Initial Teaching" and below, it shows how these are encompassed and revealed as transformations, which should be understood accordingly.
In this Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya), there is no further separate cultivation.

The commentary states: Concentration (samādhi) constitutes the essence of merit, while contemplation (vipaśyanā) serves as the foundation for wisdom. Based on this essence, the function is activated; concentration and contemplation proceed together.

Because the cause has been fulfilled and the fruit is perfected, the two feet [of merit and wisdom] are equally complete; therefore, there is no need for further cultivation of the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana).
The second [category], indefinite cultivation, extends to an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).
The commentary explains that there are two meanings to the term "indefinite *saṃkhyeya*":

first, because the realms and categories differ and the eons (*kalpa*) are likewise distinct, it does not stop at three; second, based on the boundlessness of the Buddha’s virtues, time is also limitless. If...
The statement regarding the "three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*" likely refers to those who are subject to provisional transformation.
The commentary asks: "Does this refer to those who have reached certainty or those who have not?
The explanation states: This follows upon the provisional to challenge the ultimate, thereby exhausting the reasons for the state of non-certainty.
Answer: This was stated because the previous teaching was intended for those of inferior capacity;
thus, it limited [the path] to three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* while establishing them in a state of mind directed toward this teaching.

Now, because their faculties have matured, it is shown that [the path] is not fixed, allowing for further progress toward the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Such is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Sage. Thus it is known.
If one relies on the Sudden Teaching (dun-jiao), other cases may be inferred accordingly.
The commentary states: "Time has no separate substance; it is established based upon phenomena. Since this teaching is free from characteristics (lakṣaṇa), there are no distinct temporal divisions.
First, the primary clarification concerns "one thought-moment" (ekakṣaṇa); what follows explains its characteristics.
If one follows the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), other cases may be inferred accordingly.
The commentary states: First is the heading, second is the inquiry, and third is the explanation.

Regarding the phrase "all kalpas interpenetrate" and so forth, this means that great kalpas and small kalpas interpenetrate, long kalpas and short kalpas are mutually identical, essence and function are unimpeded, and every thought-moment is perfectly interfused.
They interpenetrate one another in successive layers like the jewels of Indra’s net; at such a time, because they pervade every place, it is said that they are "comprehensive and penetrating.
Nevertheless, each subsequent phrase below demonstrates their distinct characteristics of orderly arrangement.
Regarding the fifth [topic], the body that serves as the basis for practice:

the commentary states that this marks the heading of the section. Thus, although the preceding text discussed the appropriate timing for traversing the stages of practice, if one investigates their ultimate basis, how could they be divorced from the physical vessel? Therefore, this follows next.

If, according to the Hīnayāna, this [body] is real and not a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the commentary explains that "segmented" means having limited physical parts that have not yet been entirely eliminated. Since this teaching extends from the cause to the fulfillment of the fruit, it is all this very body;
even its presiding transformer possesses this same body. Why is this so? Because it relies upon...
Because it manifests as the seeds of affliction (*kleśa*).
According to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), this is a transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and not real.
The commentary states: although the *śrāvakas* of this teaching aspire to a vast and expansive mind and direct their attention toward the Mahāyāna, they still possess afflictions.

Because they have not yet eliminated [afflictions], their physical bodies remain coarse and manifest; thus, they are also said to undergo "segmented" existence (*paricchinna*). Although the Tathāgatas manifest similar bodies in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, these are not actual retributive fruits.
If one proceeds directly upward, there is the "transformative" existence (*pariṇāmiki*) at the higher stages.

The commentary states: Because they do not pass through the stages of the lesser sages but directly resolve upon the Great Mind, it is called "direct advancement. Regarding the phrase "relying on stages" and so forth:
this means that from the first up to the seventh stage, all belong to the cultivation of conditioned effort; because these are considered coarse, they are termed "segmented.

From the eighth stage onward, there is the spontaneous nature of unconditioned reality (*asaṃskṛta-dharmatā*) and the traces of effort subside; because these are considered subtle, [they are termed "unsegmented"].

It is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) because the cause shifts and the fruit changes; it is also called "transformation" because the coarse is transformed into the subtle and the short is transformed into the long.
This is the meaning of the phrase "reaching the actual retribution."
The commentary states: First, based on the primary afflictions, two [types of birth] are established; subsequently, by examining the substance of the afflictions, three [types] are determined.

Therefore, the passage beginning with "Thus, the ten... cites a sūtra to provide proof. Since it speaks of the *antarābhava* (intermediate state), how could this not be a body of the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence)?
Question: Does this refer to the body of fragmented existence (*paricchinna-śarīra*) from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onwards?

Explanation: Previously, we discussed the body of true retribution (*vipāka-deha*); however, since the body of fragmented existence extends throughout all ten stages, when one reaches the bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above—who have eternally suppressed the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of afflictions (*kleśa*) and are thus no different from arhats—one ought to speak of the body of transformation (*nirmāṇa-deha*).
[They] again receive a body of segmented existence (*piṇḍa-śarīra*).
The answer is: "If it is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up until the point of using [it] to take birth.

The commentary states: By distinguishing between seeds (*bīja*) and active manifestations (*samudācāra*), one differentiates [the state of] ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*) who receive a body; thus, there is no contradiction regarding the suppression of latent afflictions (*anuśaya-kleśa*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states, "until it retains those seeds.

The commentary explains that "all are due to the power of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)" refers to the seeds; "continuing through successive births" refers to birth-and-death in distinct segments (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).
Furthermore, in the lower section of the *She lun* (likely referring to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*), one may see how both ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle are excluded.
The commentary states: "The Sage reaches the various stages through bodily mastery. The explanation says:
from "The commentary states" onwards, it distinguishes between ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles to determine the nature of their rebirth;

if one says [the following], it restates the objection and returns it for examination; "retaining afflictions for what purpose? addresses that [objection] while conforming to this [position], thereby establishing the correct meaning. If... [as before].

According to the lower [system], even if one allows for the transformation of the mind and the subsequent change of the body, this belongs to the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and is not a seed of affliction (*kleśa-bīja*).
Question: If that is so, why does it continue until the attainment of the changeable body (*pariṇāma-śarīra*)?

The commentary states: This question arises because the aforementioned claim—that those from the eighth bhūmi upward also receive a body of segmented birth based on the seeds of afflictions—is in extreme contradiction with the meaning of the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-avadāna* (Renwang jing) and other sacred teachings regarding the stages from the eighth bhūmi upward. Therefore, this inquiry is posed.
Answer: These [points] are briefly explained through ten gates for the sake of reaching a concise summary.
The commentary states that this is a general answer that sets forth the headings.
First, "it is said that arhats... refers to the explanation according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
The commentary states: First, it is explained below that cause and effect are equally established as having no distinction in their state.
Why is this? Because what is discussed in this teaching presents the Buddha manifesting the appearance of an old bhikṣu.

As for the Vinaya below, which indicates the place of origin and the conversion of the five men—this refers to beginning at the Deer Park and first converting Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others (and so forth). Regarding the "general and particular" mentioned here, there are six [points].
Since these are all bhikṣus, they sit together on the same level; that is, they sit together upon the *vimokṣa-bhadrāsana*. One should know that this concludes the instruction.
Furthermore, regarding the two [types of practitioners], they also differ in the degree of their attainment within the stage of Buddhahood.

The commentary states: Regarding the initial section on the relative magnitude [of the two obscurations], as illustrated by the cited passage below, this section explains that "attaining enlightenment" refers to the simultaneous abandonment of afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This means that from the initial stage of intentionally retaining afflictions until the final fulfillment of the fruit, the cognitive obscurations constitute the primary hindrance to the great wisdom of enlightenment; thus, they are addressed throughout each of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Because one cuts [the afflictions] bit by bit until they are ultimately exhausted only upon reaching Bodhi, it is metaphorically called "sudden.

Because the afflictions are extinguished and the fruit is accomplished, it is said that one "suddenly becomes" an Arhat or a Tathāgata. Alternatively, some say: "If the two obstacles are severed simultaneously, one should only become a Buddha;
why then speak of an Arhat? Herein, the lower [level] is used to illustrate the meaning of attraction and guidance regarding the afflictions.
Third, from the tenth stage up to the section on turning back the teachings for those of the two vehicles.

The commentary states: "The initial division distinguishes between the Great and the Small, as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; the subsequent reference to what is taught therein is the 'Chapter on the Four Reliances' (*Caturpratisaraṇa-parivarta*).

This passage uses the latter part [of the text] to demonstrate the underlying reason, so that those at the stage of the cause may conceive a sense of inadequacy regarding their own position and aspire toward the great fruit.
Therefore, taking both [categories] together, they all belong to the category of "attracting and gathering" (*ākarṣaṇa*).
From the fourth through the seventh stage, up to and including the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body).

The commentary states: "The initial division of Great and Small is as in the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra); below, the sūtra is cited to demonstrate the characteristics. First, the characteristics of the Small Vehicle are shown. Eight.
The "Subterranean Manifestation of the Great Signs" states that the Bodhisattva of Far-reaching Practice (Dūraṃgamā) refers to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).

From the initial dwelling of the mind in the first stage, one has traveled far until reaching the ultimate limit of effortful application; thus, the habitual tendencies of the three realms (*tridhātu-vāsanā*) are subdued.

This means that the outflows of afflictive habits (*kleśa-vāsanā-āsrava*) are eternally extinguished in their active manifestation, such that the cause is lost and the fruit is forfeited. It is in reference to this that [the stage] is equated with the level of an Arhat according to the provisional teachings.

For those who ride upon the increase of compassion, they retain their afflictions only until this stage; thus, the body of segmented birth ceases precisely here, and the cause and effect [of that body] are exhausted.
This [section] relies on the lower [stages] to distinguish the cessation of the Great and Small Vehicles according to the functional and non-functional aspects of the stages.
This [section] relies on the teachings to manifest the provisional correspondence, discussing the two bodies in relation to the two obstacles.
The first two and the third of the five stages reach the point of emerging into the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
The commentary explains that these encompass all practices and reveal the gradations of the stages: the first three stages correspond to those of humans and devas;
the fourth and fifth stages correspond to śrāvakas; the sixth stage corresponds to pratyekabuddhas; and from the seventh stage onward, they correspond to those of the Three Vehicles.

Since the term "Bodhisattva" has already been used, it encompasses all subsequent stages; this is because the explanation was given by relying on the general characteristics of the provisional vehicle (śrāvaka-yāna) for the sake of correspondence.
The phrase "this knowledge" below refers to the selection and analysis [of the text] according to the Sūtra.
The six worldly paths and those of the two vehicles are explained by distinguishing their respective characteristics.
The commentary states: This chapter, by way of contrast, is largely similar to what preceded it;

furthermore, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, it relies upon the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) to manifest the single vehicle (*ekayāna*), thereby showing that the preceding seven stages all belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) path of effort and have not yet attained [the state of] self-...

In general, these all pertain to the three vehicles; as indicated by the illustrative text cited below from the *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha), this is explained in the section on the "limits of realization" from the first bhūmi onwards. The commentary states:

with respect to their realization and entry, they transcend both the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and the śrāvaka; that is to say, those at the first bhūmi realize both the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) simultaneously.
Therefore, it is not the same as the mundane cultivation of dhyāna that merely suppresses afflictions, nor is it the same as the samādhis of the Two Vehicles which are partial and one-sided.

As the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) clarifies through its lower-level textual analysis, since it speaks of "inferential realization" (*anumāna*), we know with certainty that realization exists only from the stages (*bhūmi*) upward;
those of the Two Vehicles all possess only inferential contemplation (*anumāna-vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the eighth stage, from the three stages of worthiness up to the explanation of falling back or not falling back, the commentary states:
"In the True Teaching (Shijiao), the three stages of worthiness completely sever the defilements of delusion, which differs from the two vehicles who seek quiescence through partial truth;

therefore, it is said that [the Bodhisattvas] have already transcended [them]. This refers to the passage in the *Awakening of Faith* that clarifies the characteristics of the three stages of worthiness. Furthermore, Master Ren... [text ends].
Since the King [of Dharma] descends to belong to those at the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), that text states:

"Good son, when one first gives rise to the thought of faith, there are sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who practice and subdue themselves through patience (*kṣānti*). Within the Three Jewels, they give rise to the nature of the seeds of cultivation (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*) and the ten mental states, namely:
the mind of faith, the mind of diligence, the mind of mindfulness, and so forth. This is what constitutes a bodhisattva’s ability to transform sentient beings to a small degree."

"Having already transcended all the wholesome stages (*śubha-bhūmi*) of the two vehicles. The *Qingliang* commentary explains: "These ten minds constitute the causal stage within the nature of the cultivated seeds (*xi zhongxing*).

They serve as the causes for the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*); because the cause is distinguished from the fruit, these ten are added. One knows that by directly penetrating through delusion, one surpasses the two vehicles.

This is explained according to the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*), concerning the distinction between those who regress and those who do not; that is to say, the *Awakening of Faith* treats this in terms of non-regression."
"Surpassing the Two Vehicles" refers to the benevolent kings' position of transcending and surpassing [the lower stages].
From the "Mind of Fulfillment of the Nine Faiths" onwards, it is explained according to the One Vehicle.

The commentary states: this means that when the merit of the ten faiths of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is perfected, it suddenly encompasses the Buddha-ground; because it is utterly distinct from the Three Vehicles, it is so described.

That which transcends all [teachings] equally, such as the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (Bhadrapāla), refers to the discourse on virtuous deeds that encompasses both cause and effect in their mutual penetration;
therefore, it concludes by stating: "This is explained according to the One Vehicle."
"First, from the stage of ordinary beings up to the teaching on the Three Vehicles.
The commentary states: "Having first generated the great bodhicitta, one then unites compassion and wisdom, thereby immediately transcending the Lesser Vehicle sages.
As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, this refers to the passage where a śrāmaṇera walks on the same path as an arhat."
Mihuo suddenly gave rise to the Great Mind; an Arhat, recognizing its excellence, then yielded the place to him and moved forward.
This is because those who have attained penetration through either the One Vehicle or the Three Vehicles both transcend the Lesser Sages.
"By virtue of this [principle], one should know it by analogy.
The commentary explains that because the ten preceding gates serve as a model for all others, it says "all such explanations," etc.

Although these responses are made in relation to the question regarding the reception of a body, among them there are also those who have transcended the stages of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and rely upon a support-body (*āśraya-kāya*).
This should be understood by analogy with the *Mahāyānābhidharma-sūtra*, which states that in the seventh stage one receives a body of segmented existence (*paricchinna-deha*).
If one follows the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*), this is explained within the section on the severance of delusions at the lower stages.

The commentary states: "Regarding those who retain delusions before the stages to receive a body, this refers to those in the stage of Worthiness (*ārya*); because their vows and wisdom are inferior, they rely upon delusions."
Receiving birth serves to support their wisdom and vows; once they reach the first bhūmi, they are embraced and transformed by great compassion in an unrestricted manner.
They do not need to further retain the seeds of delusion to undergo transformation;

nor can one distinguish between the conceptual and innate types of delusion, for since false afflictions have no substantial reality, how could their coarse or subtle categories be pointed out? Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* groups the six defilements together.

If that is so regarding the two types of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) and their equalities, why does the text subsequently state: "Furthermore, within the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one further abandons a portion"?
This is because it employs a general principle to characterize that which is "without abandonment" as being "abandoned.
These coarse factors (*audārika-bhāga*) are precisely what constitutes ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* regards ignorance as the heavy burden (*dauṣṭhulya*).

Question: If [the Bodhisattva] engages in the gathering of beings through "common purpose" (samānārthatā) from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onwards, the commentary states that the Bodhisattva’s taking of birth to benefit sentient beings is sustained by the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Since it has already been stated that these are permanently severed from the first stage, the present objection asks: How can the gathering of beings through great compassion and common purpose be entirely inconsistent with the four [means of attraction]?
[This] is a summary.
Answer: From the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*) up to the attainment of mastery and co-arising.

The commentary states: When a bodhisattva cultivates the causes, their endeavor is directed toward universal salvation; yet, if their provisional teachings are of a lower rank or their vows and wisdom have not [yet matured],...

The seeds of the afflictions that serve as the sufficient and necessary conditions have now been exhausted; this marvelous state, for which there is no other means of instruction, will no longer exist.
Question: As it is said regarding the eighth stage, what is the meaning of this?
The commentary states: For Bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching (*neyārtha*), from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, their compassion (*karuṇā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) differ.

Those with compassion remain with afflictions (*kleśa*) to moisten rebirth and receive a body of segmented existence (*paricchinna-śarīra*); those with wisdom suppress and sever [afflictions] to advance toward seeking a body of transformation (*pariṇāmika-śarīra*).

When they reach the eighth stage, compassion and wisdom are no longer distinct; therefore, it is here said that this applies only to those from the eighth stage downward. Since for them [the former] has increased exclusively, [the distinction remains].
"How does this differ from the present? Therefore, it asks: 'What is the meaning of this? The answer is:
'As has been explained thus, to what extent is it called "predominance" (adhipati)?

The commentary states: This is a critique of partiality based on the ultimate reality; therefore, it says, "I fear it may not be so. Why? Because the following section interrogates and explains the error of partiality."

First, the explanation of the fault of compassion being predominant: this is a failure resulting from attachment and views. [The text] first permits the simultaneous operation of compassion and wisdom, and subsequently refutes it, stating:
"If it is not even called 'predominant' when compassion is superior, how much less so when it is supported by inferior wisdom? Next, the explanation of the fault of wisdom being predominant:

this is a failure resulting from sinking into emptiness while remaining conjoined with existence. The structure of these refutations—consisting of permission and subsequent withdrawal—is omitted in the text, but the pattern follows the previous example.
Therefore [it is so]. [The question:
"Do the various bodhisattvas reach a state where there is increase or decrease?

The commentary explains: "By the various [bodhisattvas]" and below clarifies the Great Practice of Non-abiding; "like a chariot" and below uses a metaphor to manifest the simultaneous cultivation of both.
Regarding the phrase "from the beginning," it means that from the very moment the bodhicitta is first generated, compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem.

Because there is compassion, the Bodhisattva differs from the Hinayana practitioner who is mired in stagnant quiescence; because there is wisdom, they differ from the ordinary person who drifts in samsara.
Since they are distinct from these two, their practice achieves non-abiding.
It should be understood that by means of this, one attains mutual increase.

The commentary explains: regarding the teaching, the two types of death are established because there are differences between the coarse and the subtle at the beginning and end. As for the statement that there are two kinds of birth and death:

this refers to receiving the "segmented" (*paricchinna*) death through the coarseness of afflictions (*kleśa*), and receiving the "transformational" (*pariṇāma*) death through the subtlety of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

It is not that compassion and wisdom do not mutually increase one another. If that were so, it would not only mean that both must be cultivated together in the definitive teachings (nītārtha), but also that they cannot be practiced in isolation even within the provisional teachings (neyārtha).
If one were to say that their wisdom reaches the state of non-differentiation, [it would follow that compassion does as well].
The commentary states: This citation of the defense involves both concession and refutation. It means that this defense claims:

"Regarding what was previously critiqued as being 'unfit for discussion,' let us concede that while compassion and wisdom are predominant, there is no fault in saying that a Bodhisattva whose wisdom is predominant has small-vehicle tendencies and fears their former habits;

since these are permanently suppressed by wisdom, what fault is there in saying that wisdom is predominant? If, in the following section, one considers those prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), this observation takes into account inferior practice as a concession.
From the first bhūmi onward, [the text] refutes [other views] by means of the superior practices of realized wisdom, both above and below;

this is consistent with the critique of partiality, as both belong to the stage of the grounds (bhūmi). Therefore, it can be understood that in the *Awakening of Faith*, the section on the "inferior" refers exclusively to the teaching of realization.
Furthermore, in this teaching, "also as indicated below" refers to the eighth section, which clarifies the stages by means of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The commentary states that "also as indicated below" is explained within the eighth gate, which reveals the stages by means of the delusions. Thus, that text says:
"By means of the habitual tendencies of the four obstacles, the four stages of the *bhūmi*, the four concentrations (*samādhi*), the four virtues, and the four retributions are revealed."
[And so forth. If one relies on the Sudden Teaching (dun jiao), as explained in the Śrī-bhāga section, the commentary states:
"Since no stages are established, there is neither body nor mind; there is only numinous stillness."
This is because, according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one reaches this stage while still at the level of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).

The commentary explains that what is discussed in this teaching does not differentiate between the characteristics of the transformation body (*pariṇāma-kāya*) and the分段身 (*fen-duan-shen*, *bheda-kāya*).

This means that for those of the perfect capacity on the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), defilements and obscurations are suddenly eliminated; they perfectly create inconceivable afflictions without the distinction of gradual destruction, and their bodies lack the differentiation of coarse and subtle.
Because of these differences, Sudhana exhaustively investigates the cause and realizes the fruit within a single lifetime.
Question: Why is it that here [the text] reaches this point, while the remainder is to be understood by analogy?
Explanation: There are two questions and two answers; in the answers, the world-sphere nature and so forth are indicated as being of a similar class regarding their subtle bodily characteristics.
Why is it that while *pariṇāma-śarīra* (transformation-death) is discussed, only *bheda-śarīra* (segmentation-death) is addressed?

It is because the teaching is established through the principle of "the lower overcoming the higher. Regarding delusion, since one is deluded in all things, delusion constitutes a single boundary of affliction;
regarding awakening, since one awakens in all things, faith being fulfilled suddenly overturns that very boundary.
