The sixth section, "The Delimitation of the Abandonment of Afflictions," extends to the characteristics of the stages manifested by entrusting the afflictions.

The commentary states: Regarding the delimitation of the abandonment of afflictions discussed here, it refers to the fact that because one relies on awakening, confusion is based upon that [awakening];

yet, since one speaks of awakening based on that confusion, and because the afflictions have coarse and subtle degrees, there are differences in the excellence or subtlety of wisdom according to the variations in the teachings. This is explained according to the lower section of the chapters.
The first [point] is based on the person, while the second refers to the shallow and deep stages of the distinct positions.

Regarding the first meaning: if one relies on the afflictive and cognitive hindrances (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*), the commentary states that it is precisely because this teaching discusses the manifest realization of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) that it fully possesses the characteristics of the delusions of the three vehicles.

This highlights the distinction between those who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] and those who proceed directly. Regarding the "obstructions" mentioned below, although the essence of delusion is severed stage by stage, it essentially consists of only two types.
First, we distinguish the two vehicles' severance, which extends up to the tenth [stage], namely the clinging to precepts and prohibitions (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The commentary states: Regarding "the first" and "the beginning," these refer to their names and numbers. "Arising simultaneously" (sahaja) distinguishes between the coarse and the subtle;
collectively there are ten types. First, "attachment" (*rāga*) has craving within the three realms as its essence, and its function is to produce manifold suffering.

As for "producing manifold suffering," it means that through the power of craving, the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*) arise. Second, "aversion" (*pratigha*) [is directed] toward sentient beings and their suffering, and...
The faculty of suffering has aversion and resentment as its essence; its function is to serve as the basis for unpeaceful abiding and for unwholesome conduct.
"Unpeaceful abiding" means that because the mind harbors aversion and resentment, one dwells frequently in suffering.
Ignorance refers to the lack of wisdom regarding the three realms as its essence; it serves as the basis for the arising of false certainties, doubt, and afflictions with respect to all phenomena.

Karma refers to the arising of various afflictions through ignorance. The four types of pride (*māna*) have the nature of mental exaltation based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and their function is to serve as the basis for the arising of disrespect.

Disrespect means giving rise to arrogance toward teachers, elders, and those possessed of virtue. The arising of suffering means the production of future existence (*punarbhava*). Fifth, doubt (*vicikitsā*) regarding...

Its essence is doubt regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*), and its function is the cessation of the arising of wholesome states. "Doubt regarding the principles of the truths" includes doubt regarding the [Three] Jewels.
"The non-arising of wholesome states" means that due to indecision, one does not engage in cultivation.

As for the six types of view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): they are the various forms of acceptance (*kṣānti*) consisting of the observation and grasping of a self and what belongs to a self with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).

The essence consists of the resolve, investigation, view, and insight [regarding permanence or annihilation]; its function is to serve as the basis for all types of views. Regarding the seven extreme views:

they take as their essence the various forms of acceptance, resolve, investigation, view, and insight that, in relation to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) and so forth, observe and grasp them as either permanent or annihilated.

Their function is to obstruct the middle way and the departure [from suffering]. As for those who practice the middle way: this refers to those who, free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, rely upon dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The eight wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) have as their essence the denial of cause, the denial of effect, and the denial of function; or they consist of clinging to real entities or false conceptualization.
Their function is the severing of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and their further function is to serve as the basis for the firmness of the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
The ninth, the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), refers to [the attachment] toward all views and the five aggregates that are the basis of those views.

The nature of the view of grasping at aggregates and so forth consists in observing them as supreme, excellent, superior, or sublime, and taking this as the basis for various forms of patience, desire, thought, examination, and views;

its function is to serve as the support for incorrect views. The ten types of grasping at precepts and observances consist in observing various precepts and observances, as well as the five aggregates of grasping that serve as their basis, and taking them as purification and liberation.
The essence of the "observance of rules and rituals" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists in the views, desires, discursive thoughts, and investigations directed toward [wrong] forms of renunciation;

its function is to serve as a basis for weariness that is without fruit. Regarding "rules and rituals," this refers to being preceded by wrong views; it is "weariness without fruit" because one cannot thereby achieve liberation.
Among these, four are coarse while two are innate.

The commentary explains: they are distinguished as coarse because they manifest clearly, whereas the innate ones are subtle and difficult to perceive; therefore, they arise simultaneously with the body and perform the same function as the mind.
Among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), these four are exclusively coarse and exclusively restricted to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), while the remaining six are otherwise.
Because they encompass both the coarse and the subtle, they pertain to both types [of arising].
From the arising of the five consciousnesses up to the arising of conceptualization.

The commentary states: The following distinguishes the extent to which the various consciousnesses possess afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Regarding the phrase "the first three," these refer to greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth.

Ignorance—these three are of an unwholesome nature, and thus they exist within the five consciousnesses. As for the three causes, such as wrong teachers and so forth, which arise from the lower [realms]:

because they are induced by these three [unwholesome roots], they belong to the category of discrimination (*vikalpa*). Wrong teachers, wrong teachings, and wrong reflection are called "wrong" because they are led by those three [roots].
Therefore, they pertain to discrimination.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses ten types [of discrimination]: four types of discrimination, six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and two [others].
The commentary states: because the arising of the mental consciousness is even more extensive and it still relies upon the other consciousnesses, it thus universally possesses [all these].
The manas-consciousness possesses only four; therefore, it possesses only four.
The commentary states: The first phrase correctly clarifies [the point]; the second phrase excludes [other possibilities].

The reason for excluding hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth is that the *manas*—here translated as "defiled mind," referring to the seventh consciousness—is exclusively associated with the obscuring (*nivṛta*) [afflictions] and thus lacks hatred.

Furthermore, the exclusion of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is because it is "of a single class" (*ekajātīya*) and "continuously flows" (*prabandhena pravartate*), taking the eighth consciousness as its object.

One might raise the objection: "Since there is the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) which clings to the ālayavijñāna as its object, there must necessarily be the extreme view of 'mine' (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
To this, the present text replies: "Because one is occupied moment by moment with clinging to a self, there is no leisure for [the view of] extremes; therefore, there is no extreme view.

Furthermore, among the latter three [categories], those that are distinguished from the other four *anuśayas* by arising in dependence upon three causes are definitely categorized as conceptual (*vikalpita*).

This consciousness lacks those [object-conditions] because it is exclusively co-emergent (*sahaja*), and thus does not give rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, an objection is raised:

"Since it belongs to the category of the co-emergent, how does it differ from the first five consciousnesses, which also possess a co-emergent aspect? Therefore, the text now distinguishes it by stating:
"Furthermore, because it is constantly continuous and takes [the ālayavijñāna] as its object, it is not induced by the sixth consciousness," and so forth.
Regarding its eighth consciousness reaching the state of the indeterminate (avyākṛta):

the commentary explains that because the eight consciousnesses are pure and stainless, free from afflictions and latent tendencies (anuśaya), they do not arise as a whole [in that state] and are exclusively maturation (vipāka).
This means they are merely the sovereign of the collective retribution.
These [afflictions] include both the discriminative and the innate, totaling one hundred and twenty-eight.

The commentary explains that their number is determined according to the realms and stages; because they universally delude one regarding the Four Noble Truths, they differ from those of the Hīnayāna.
First the discriminative are clarified, followed by the innate; combining these with the preceding lower categories, the total number of afflictions can be understood.
Question: For what reason does the previously mentioned ignorance regarding phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) extend to all objects?

Explanation: Regarding the question of whether [ignorance] is pervasive or limited, there is one question and two answers. Within the question, according to a verse from the *Abhidharmakośa* of the Hīnayāna:

"In the stage of suffering (*duḥkha*), it possesses all [objects]; in the stages of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*), three [types of views] are excluded; in the path (*mārga*), two [types of views] are excluded; and it does not function in the higher realms."

Because of this resentment, the present objection states that the ten *anuśayas* do not pertain to delusion regarding the Four Truths; this is an objection made by restricting [the scope] in order to challenge the comprehensive [view].

In the response, there are two points: first, it addresses the breadth of the afflictions (*kleśa*); second, it relies on the fact that objects are solely mental phenomena, for since they arise through the transformation of the mind, delusion is comprehensive.
The intent is to distinguish this from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) view that objects exist externally to the mind.
The second [stage] involves abandoning the afflictions until one attains the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).

The commentary states that "abandoning afflictions and attaining the fruit" refers to the distinctions in the stages of realization and entry resulting from the varying degrees of afflictions to be eliminated.
First, regarding the abandonment of conceptualized afflictions, there are three different types of entry into the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). As for the first type, at the beginning...
In the final moment preceding the fruit, one suddenly severs the one hundred and twelve categories of conceptual discrimination regarding the truths that delude the three realms,
thereby realizing the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Second, as for the "one who has doubly departed from desire," this refers to one who comes from among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and,
while among them, previously suppressed the first six of the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm through the practice of the six preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
Thereafter, they turn their minds toward the Buddha and give rise to the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), entering the Path of True Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

By severing conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) and simultaneously severing the six grades of afflictions previously suppressed during the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), they realize the second fruit.

Thus it is said that by "severing in addition" and "leaving desire twice," one attains the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*). The phrase "leaving desire twice" explains the characteristics more clearly; since both matters are removed together, it is called "twice."
Furthermore, regarding the third type—those who have already abandoned desire—they also come from among humans or non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
However, within those paths, they have previously used the six preparatory practices (*prayoga*) to equally suppress the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm through cultivation;

subsequently, they turn their minds toward the Buddha, cultivate the contemplation of self-emptiness (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), enter the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), and thereby sever both conceptual and [innate] afflictions.

Because one realizes the three fruits by means of the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that have been subdued, they are called "Non-returners" (*anāgāmin*);

because they do not return, it is said that they have already become free from desire (*vītarāga*). As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this is because they have reached the realization of the three fruits.

The commentary states: The three preceding categories of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) practitioners enter realization based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; therefore, these three are cited as evidence.
Next, they sever the innate [afflictions] up to the fruit of Arhatship.

The commentary states: Since the seven consciousnesses arising simultaneously are severed last, it is now said that the six consciousnesses arising simultaneously consist of nine grades across nine stages—meaning there are nine grades for each of the nine stages within the three realms, totaling eighty-one grades.
Furthermore, regarding the practitioner who advances in cultivation, this refers to those described as the first category of persons who have attained the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Thus, regarding those previously seen who are to gradually attain deliverance through this correct practice, the rest is as explained in the usual [treatises].
Second, as for those who attain deliverance all at once (*sakṛd-vyutthāna*): it refers to reaching the point where no further fruit remains.

The commentary explains that they are called "sudden" because they do not pass through the stages sequentially; that is to say, this class of persons, by virtue of their superior faculties (*indriya*), [attains it directly].
Therefore, the eighty-one grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the three realms are grouped into three sets of nine.

Because one simultaneously abandons the first grade of the desire realm, the first grade of the form realm, and the first grade of the formless realm at once, it is said that "the three realms are abandoned all at once" (*sakṛt-prahāṇa*).
Subsequently, one abandons the second, third, and so forth, up to the ninth grade; thus, it is said that "the nine grades are gradually eliminated" (*krama-śas-prahāṇa*).
These two [paths] and the third are likewise abandoned simultaneously across the three realms;

however, because one cultivates this abandonment and realization within the body of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and proceeds directly to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) without further passing through the second or third fruits, it is said that "there are no further fruits remaining."
"What is this? It refers to the gradual removal [of afflictions] up to the Cloud of Dharma.

The commentary explains that this investigates and clarifies the sudden and gradual [approaches]. Regarding the vertical discussion, it does not contradict the sequential removal of the nine grades [of afflictions].
If that is so, why is it stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna* and other treatises as previously explained?

The commentary explains: "If that is so" (*yadi tarhi*) introduces the question; "because [it is] below" provides the answer. Thus, the phrase from the *Abhidharma* (*Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda*) serves as the proof.

"If that is so" restates the objection regarding sudden transcendence (*sakṛd-vyutthāna*), for its gradual abandonment cannot involve the simultaneous cognition (*sakṛd-ālambana*) of the phenomena (*dharma*) of the three realms.

This correct answer clarifies the intent of the question: since those with dull faculties firmly adhere to gradual progression, how could they possibly abandon [the afflictions] instantaneously if they do not perceive them instantaneously?
The Abhidharma text clearly states that "relying on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*)" means relying on the preparatory stage of the desire realm prior to the fundamental dhyāna of the form realm.
This is because the afflictions of that *manas* are severed upon its arrival [at the final stage].
The commentary states: Since the seven consciousnesses function continuously, their afflictions are subtle; therefore, they cannot be abandoned all at once.

Furthermore, because the wisdom and conduct of those who have attained transcendence are also superior, they cannot take them as objects all at once. Thus, within the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), they are abandoned simultaneously with the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Because it has been severed, the proof in the lower *Yogācārabhūmi* is not like the following selection and clarification; this should be understood accordingly. Question:
For what reason does the aforementioned ignorance exist within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?

Explanation: Because ignorant *śrāvakas* merely sever [defilements] by distinguishing between realms, they lack this sudden transcendence; therefore, the question follows upon that point to raise the objection.
[The text] answers this by clarifying that from the inferior [state] up to the abandonment of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The commentary states: First, superior wisdom draws forth and transforms that small mind; second, through two types of analogies, it reveals that the *manas* is limited in its teaching.
"Inferior to this" refers to the limit of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
As for the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they persist until the state of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The commentary explains: because these cognitive obstructions can only obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they must be severed and extinguished at the time of entering the remainderless nirvāṇa (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
Because its wisdom alone is manifest and without remainder, it is exclusively non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
All other matters are as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. The commentary states:

previously, both types were indicated together under "liberation through wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukti*); here, two categories are listed. Since that which is to be known by this vehicle is uniquely obstructed [by ignorance], [it is distinguished].
Since meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not obstruct wisdom (*prajñā*), those liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) do not abandon it.

As for those called "liberated by both" (*ubhaya-to-bhāga-vimukta*), it refers to the dual cultivation of concentration and wisdom; because concentration is obstructed and they have not attained liberation through it, they must abandon it.
This refers to the eight lower [fetters], which indicate the obstructions to be abandoned and the wisdom that abandons them.
Furthermore, regarding "all liberations," they attain liberation through the attainment of mastery.
The commentary states: the first phrase refers to the eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); the second phrase indicates freedom from obstacles;
and the subsequent portion clarifies their profound penetration by way of the human body and its obstacles.
One should know that this Initial Teaching [extends] up to the severance of seeds.
The commentary states: Within this, there are two senses in which the connection and selection are made:

first, selection by way of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), meaning that while the Hīnayāna severs only afflictions (*kleśa*), this [teaching] severs both afflictions and the objects of knowledge; second, [the distinction that] the Hīnayāna severs only afflictions.
This, then, simultaneously severs the seeds. Why is this so? It is because that Hīnayāna school does not discuss the eight consciousnesses containing [seeds], and thus lacks seeds;
even if they were to posit them, such as the Sautrāntika school does, they would simply belong to the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva proceeding directly reaches the point where both obstacles are severed.
The commentary states: although this teaching distinguishes between the five stages of suppression and severance, these are all [deals with] the two obstacles;
thus, unlike the Śrāvakas, they are not further divided by realms or stages.
Furthermore, regarding the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa) up to their classification by realm (dhātu), the commentary states:
for a bodhisattva, because their contemplative wisdom (vipaśyanā-jñāna) is superior to that [of the śrāvaka], they do not need to laboriously distinguish the number of categories;
there is only a single subduing and severing.
"However, regarding the two obstacles, [the practitioner] reaches the point of suddenly severing their seeds.

The commentary explains: "Those who suppress the obstacles prior to the stages" means that within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), one suppresses the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the two obstacles, and within the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), one suppresses the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles;
in both cases, the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) serves as the means of suppression. As soon as one ascends to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), [the seeds are severed].
Upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the seeds of the two obstructions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpavāsanā*) are severed instantaneously in a single moment.
As for those [seeds] that are innate (*sahaja*), they persist until the attainment of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

The commentary states: First, it clarifies the "retention of delusions" (*kleśasthiti*). Why is this? It is because [the Bodhisattva retains them] to nourish rebirth and to gather and transform sentient beings; thus, they serve as a support.
If their wisdom and vows do not fall into the two vehicles, they protect those who have sunk into emptiness;
since the cognitive obstructions hinder great wisdom and bodhi, those who cultivate bodhi sever them bit by bit.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* extends [its analysis] up to the realization of the Buddha-fruit.
The commentary states: It is precisely by retaining the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that one initiates superior practice;
that is to say, one accumulates the sublime practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and through the mutual guidance of compassion and wisdom, one attains the untainted fruit of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, in the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty, it states that one reaches the stage of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama*).
The commentary explains: "According to this treatise, one intentionally retains the afflictions (*kleśa*) until the causes are exhausted. Why is this? The treatise says:
"One retains the afflictions until they are completely exhausted, thereby realizing the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."
The obstacles to knowledge (jñeyāvaraṇa) are only completely exhausted upon reaching that [final stage].
The commentary states: That which directly obstructs the bodhisattva path refers to those factors whose essential nature is diametrically opposed to great enlightenment (mahābodhi);
therefore, they are severed stage by stage until they reach final exhaustion at the stage of Buddhahood.
"By this, it is said that one reaches the Buddha-ground together with [the exhaustion of] what-is-to-be-known.
The commentary explains: "By this" refers to the aforementioned objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

If this is so, then because the afflictions (*kleśa*) are the objects of cultivation to be abandoned, while the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are the objects of cultivation to be relinquished, for this reason, one reaches the Buddha-ground together with them.

Therefore, because the *Abhidharmakośa* states that [the obstacles] reach [their limit] at the stage of the Tathāgata, the commentary explains that both obstacles are proven to coexist until the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).

The reason why, during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one cultivates only the path that serves as the antidote to the cognizable objects (*jñeya*) is precisely because this obstacle obstructs one's bodhi; for this reason, one cultivates the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
When one counters them with wisdom, the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) do not obstruct bodhi; because they still serve as a support for the great vow, they are not severed.
However, upon reaching the exhaustion [of these hindrances] and attaining the fruit, they perish simultaneously, and one suddenly becomes an Arhat or a Tathāgata.

This means that from the perspective of the exhaustion of afflictions, one becomes an Arhat, and from the perspective of the exhaustion of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one becomes a Tathāgata. This is merely a provisional designation.
This refers to the meaning of "attracting and gathering.
That *manas* which arises simultaneously [with the other consciousnesses] persists until the attainment of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).
The commentary states: because the seven consciousnesses that arise simultaneously specifically obstruct the Buddha-ground, they are exhausted upon reaching it.
Question: Regarding these two obstructions, what are their similarities and differences in terms of their manifestation (*samudācāra*)?

The commentary states: Since the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertaining to the two obstructions pervade all stages, when they arise and manifest within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, are they the same or different?
Answer: Their afflictions reach the point where they no longer give rise to faults and calamities.

The commentary states: Although [the afflictions] should have been exhausted, they are intentionally retained; thus they become a source of harm. Furthermore, by employing wisdom to exercise control over them, one achieves great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
"Just as a venomous snake, upon arrival, serves other purposes.

The commentary states that this is an illustration: the venomous snake represents the afflictions (*kleśa*), the power of the mantra represents wisdom (*jñāna*), and "controlling others" represents the assistance in accomplishing vows and practices.
Below, the analogy is applied to the Dharma.
"Bodhisattvas, through their skillful means, attain mastery over all.

The commentary states: First, the citation of scriptural evidence is provided; "therefore" below concludes the intended meaning. It says: "Alternatively, 'manifesting' refers to assisting in superior practice;
alternatively, 'seeding' refers to cutting off [afflictions] yet not severing [the continuity]. By means of this, they attain mastery over all.
Regarding the seventh consciousness, it is interrupted by the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
The commentary states: It does not cause rebirth in the three realms because the afflictions of the seventh consciousness are incapable of doing so;

since they do not moisten rebirth (*upapatti-sneha*), they do not sustain the process of maturation. Furthermore, their mode of activity (*ākāra*) is subtle, meaning that the four delusions arise simultaneously with it.
Since these delusions are so subtle that they manifest immediately whenever the wisdom of contemplation falters even slightly,
it is said that from the seventh bhūmi onward they occasionally manifest for brief periods, being interrupted by the wisdom of contemplation.
Regarding the statement, "Because the obstacles to what is known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed stage by stage":

the commentary explains that the two types of consciousness that take what is known as their object constitute the primary obstacles to awakening. When one desires to realize a subsequent stage and enters the mind [of that stage], it is necessary to sever them while emerging from the mind of the preceding stage;
therefore, it is said that "the afflictions of the subsequent stage all arise within the preceding stage," and so forth.
Question: If that is so, why does it reach the outflow-tainted mind and so forth?
Explanation: "If that is so" refers to the question posed by way of the successive severance of each stage (bhūmi).
The intention is that if there were a severance part by part, there should be no loss [of the fruit]; why then does the following present a contradiction as a formal objection?
Answer: If one considers the sixth [consciousness], it appears to be with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The commentary states: because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the six consciousnesses remain, that which arises appears as if not in conflict with what is to be abandoned.
If one considers the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), these two extend throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

The commentary states: Since the objects known by these two consciousnesses pervade all ten stages (*bhūmi*), if they were to arise as outflows (*sāsrava*), they would be precisely what is to be abandoned;
what further question could there be?
As for the afflictions of the *manas*, other meanings may be inferred accordingly.

The commentary states: Since the afflictions of the seven consciousnesses are not what is retained, they are substantially existent outflows (*sāsrava*). Regarding these seven stages, there are or are not the afflictions of the seven consciousnesses;

the ever-active ignorance (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-avidyā*) is constant from the very beginning. Although the two wisdoms (*jñāna*) together take both as their object, they definitively illuminate them separately:

when illuminating the Truth (*tattva*), it is tranquil and unmoving; when illuminating the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), it recognizes the distinctions of delusion. This is because [the conventional] is indeterminate.
However, it is merely a matter of the interruption and continuity of the wisdom of insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
Furthermore, in this teaching, up to the point where the Abhidharma-śāstra explains it,
the commentary states that the cessation of afflictions and the arising of wisdom are like the simultaneous rising and falling of the two ends of a scale.
Furthermore, regarding this intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it exists in the place where one is to be reborn according to the principle of the rising and falling of the two ends of a scale.
Some texts state: "As it rises, it presses down; as it presses down, it rises," or "As it builds up, it presses down;
as it presses down, it builds up. These are likely scribal errors, as they contradict the treatises.
Furthermore, regarding this obstructing dharma, it constitutes an obstruction at that point.

The commentary states: For the time being, according to the perspective of the Dharma-lakṣaṇa Mahāyāna, there exist real afflictions (*kleśa*) that can be severed; once these afflictions are extinguished, wisdom arises.

This is like the simultaneous rising and falling of the two ends of a scale. Now, using a single point to illustrate the meaning in accordance with the *Xìngxìng* (Nature-accordance) school, it is said that since [the afflictions] are already obstructions...
The meaning is that consciousness is fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and being without intrinsic nature is itself emptiness;

it is only through delusion that this is spoken of as an "obstruction. If one investigates even more deeply, the consciousness which serves as the basis also lacks intrinsic nature. Therefore, Master Guishan said, "Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream.
The phrase "consciousness is without intrinsic nature" used here also contains this same meaning; reflect upon it.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, one should understand this by referring to that text.
The commentary explains: because one realizes that suffering is without suffering, it is called "penetratingly comprehending emptiness"; this is the meaning of "this is suffering.

Now, regarding the meaning of these hindrances, if one understands them by referring to that same text, then through that one will clarify this: one penetrates the fact that the fundamental nature of afflictions and hindrances is empty.
"If one relies on the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), it reaches the point of being able to sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The commentary explains: "That which is severed by this teaching must first realize that the substance of the delusions to be abandoned is fundamentally empty, and then know that the true nature is fundamentally existent.

Only then, compared to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), does one transcend the mere maintenance of samādhis based on longing and aversion; for they have not yet understood the source of delusion, and thus they are only able [to achieve what the two vehicles do]."
I rejoice in and submit to this teaching, which seizes power by means of reality and speaks thus.
Therefore, the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* also states as above. The commentary explains:
tracing the origin of delusion regarding truth and attachment to falsehood, these two aspects are universally pervasive; even if those of the Two Vehicles aspire toward them...
How can one sever deluded attachments when they are so few? This is because the subject and object do not correspond. Qingliang said:
"When one is deluded regarding the Truth, deluded thoughts arise; when one awakens to the Truth, deluded thoughts cease. Since it is not otherwise than this, one need only subdue them.
Question: For what reason is it said that this [teaching] differs because it reaches even the dharma of the most foolish?

Explanation: There are two questions and two answers. In the first question, there are two parts: first, the teaching for the Two Vehicles which involves actual severance; second, this teaching which merely suppresses.

Because suppression and severance differ, it is necessary to establish this dialogue. In the answer, there are two parts: first, the provisional, and second, the real. Within the provisional, the phrase "above" refers to the superior [stages].

The "inferior" refers to the fact that, by relying on [the teachings] for the sake of attracting and gathering [beings], it is said that the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are severed at the same stage as the two vehicles, namely the Buddha-ground.

Furthermore, the "inferior" being "equal to the superior" means that, in order to cause them to possess further progress and permit their realization of the general path of the Great Vehicle, it is said that there is something to be severed within the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Now, regarding the phrase "this is according to reality," it investigates how those who have created such a mind are unable [to realize it].
Since Qishi has not yet awakened to the mind, how could he exhaust all delusions? Therefore, he merely employs suppression;
furthermore, his discourse on gradual progression is also inherently different.
As for the Bodhisattvas, they reach ultimate purity.
The commentary states: This teaching is for the practitioner who knows the truth and penetrates the delusion;

because there is no interruption yet there is an interruption of non-interruption, the nature of delusion is itself the nature of wisdom. Since it is thus severed, there is no obstruction to the deluded true essence.

Because delusion is already such, one does not distinguish between the co-emergent (*sahaja*) and the discriminative (*vikalpita*), nor between their coarse and subtle aspects. Why? Because it is not like the Dharma-characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*) view, which holds that there are real delusions.
Because they can be divided, there are only those that overcome [the lower]; the manifestation of the delusions (*kleśa*) consists only of these two types of "active propensities" (*paryavasthāna*).

Furthermore, when one speaks of the active propensities together with their basis—the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*)—this refers exclusively to ignorance. Regarding the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, the suppression of the active propensities and their manifestations means that "suppression" is equivalent to "abandonment.

This implies that while the afflictions (*kleśa*) are suppressed and abandoned, the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are merely set aside. If there were only suppression, [it would not constitute true abandonment].
What is meant by "the noble first stage (ārya-prathamā bhūmi) severing the seeds of the latent tendencies (anuśaya-bīja), attaining mastery over transformation, and no longer remaining [in saṃsāra]"?
Therefore, from the first stage upward, one merely eliminates the subtle habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of ignorance;

reaching the Buddha-stage, because one has departed from even the most subtle conceptualization (manas), one attains the nature of mind, which is eternally abiding—this is called ultimate awakening (atyanta-bodhi). Such elimination and severance is likewise not... [end of fragment].
This differs from other schools, which have historically refuted [this position] across forty-two distinct chapters.
However, since those stages prior to the grounds (the three levels of the "Worthy") reach as far as the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and so forth, the commentary states:
"These Bodhisattvas of the three levels of worthiness are first, those who transcend the provisional; second, those who diminish the small; and third, those who [practice] the three contemplations."

The clarity and purity of the non-duality of the ultimate and conventional truths is precisely what transcends expedient means; thus, by retaining the seeds of afflictions and severing only the cognitive obstructions, one is distinct from the Lesser Vehicle.

Therefore, it is said that [the Bodhisattva] "does not fall" and so forth. Although the text mentions only the sense of being distinct from the Lesser Vehicle, it implicitly contains the meaning of transcending expedient means. Why is this?
Because they have realized the differences between dharmas.
Therefore, the *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty [states that] "all" refers to this very meaning.

The commentary explains: although these one sūtra and two śāstras all serve as evidence that there is superior progress even prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), the *She lun* proves it differs from the Hīnayāna, while the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) proves the retention of afflictions;
the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith) provides clear proof of entering superior progress. Although the sūtras and śāstras [differ],...
In reality, this mentions one while encompassing the rest.
By means of this Bodhisattva [the fear of the cognitive hindrance], it extends even until both [hindrances] are exhausted.
The commentary states: "By means of this Bodhisattva who fears only the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—this hindrance obstructs his bodhi. This refers to that [Bodhisattva].
The fruit sought by Bodhisattvas is therefore feared; the wisdom that can remedy this consists of the contemplations of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only) and *tathatā* (suchness).
What is called "consciousness-only" refers to the contemplation of the characteristics of names, objects, intrinsic nature, and distinctions.
As for the contemplation of suchness, one should know that it is mind-only and that there are no external objects; through these two contemplations, one remedies that [object].

When wisdom is realized, delusions disperse and the empty clarity becomes the single true limit (*ekam satyadhātu*). However, because this occurs at the initial stage, it remains as a resource for practice.

On the first ground (*bhūmi*), both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are eliminated together without distinguishing between those of seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*); from the second ground onward, one eliminates only the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), and thus there is no further distinction to be made.
Therefore, the passage from the *Questions of Maitreya* cited here serves as proof.

The commentary explains: First, a small-scale example is cited to illustrate the great inquiry regarding their differences; second, the response serves to prove that true contemplation benefits sentient beings according to their capacities.
It is because afflictive obstructions are contrary to true reality, whereas coessential great compassion benefits sentient beings, that [the former] is seen [as an obstacle].
All [afflictions] on the Path are completely severed.
As for the afflictions of the *manas*, their residual habits (*vāsanā*) are eliminated later.
The commentary states: "Severing the coarse" in the first stage refers to the seeds (*bīja*); "eliminating the residual habits" refers to the stages from the second ground upward.
It merely severs the remaining residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* does not mention "severing" again thereafter.

The commentary explains that this indicates that at the time of the initial clear observation (*abhisamaya*), the seeds of the seven consciousnesses and their underlying propensities (*anuśaya*) have already been severed; from that point onward, one merely eliminates the remnants.
Because of habitual practice, there is the expression "transformation.
If one asks, "If this is 'entry,' what is meant by 'transformation and purification'?
The commentary states: This restates the objection and returns it as a counter-question to establish the meaning through ultimate proof.
If one relies on the Initial Teaching (śīkṣā), it may be as stated there.

The commentary says: This is a concession to the provisional [teaching] for the sake of resolving the objection. Why? Because in the provisional teaching, the seven consciousnesses are severed only at the stage of Buddhahood.
Therefore, one should know that this extends until the mere elimination of the residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The commentary states: From the perspective of ultimate reality, this is a definitive refutation that does not allow for the first stage to merely suppress [afflictions] temporarily;
it is certain that these are severed, with only residual habitual tendencies remaining to be eliminated later. Therefore, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* speaks of "the obstacle of habitual tendencies."
The commentary states that the treatise clarifies three categories, each first identifying a fault and subsequently pointing to the delusions associated with specific individuals;
the primary category serves to substantiate the preceding passage concerning the latencies (*vāsanā*) on the stages (*bhūmi*).
The explanation says: "The treatise explains [the phrase] 'latencies produced immediately prior'."
The commentary states: Because their stage is increasingly high and their afflictions are increasingly attenuated, those on the stages (bhūmi) are called *mahāsattvas*.

Thus, it is known that there exists only the obstacle of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). As for "habitual tendencies," this refers to the portion of the perfuming influence of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*).
Question: How is it that from the first bhūmi upward, one loses this [attainment] and it no longer exists therein?

Explanation: There are two answers to the initial question. The question concerns the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*), while the brief answer is based on the simultaneous removal of both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

As stated below, by citing the sudden transcendence of the lesser sages (śrāvakas), the text illustrates the extraordinary excellence of the *sattva* (bodhisattva), saying that [the former] "cannot even attain" it.

Regarding that fruit of a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin): it is said that because one ascends directly to the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa), one does not realize the fruit of a Once-returner [at that time].
Furthermore, in this teaching, the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* states:

"The commentary explains that knowing the arising of afflictions and their cessation is neither at the beginning, the middle, nor the end" means that because there is no interruption, they have the nature of being mutually conditioned (*ālambana*).
Since the fundamental is fused yet severed, the delusions that obscure the truth must be eliminated. Why? This interrogates the metaphor:
the emptiness of delusion is like the primordial purity of the great void.
Furthermore, this should be understood as it pertains to this teaching.
The commentary states: When delusion regarding the truth gives rise to false thoughts, the truth follows along with the delusions.

Therefore, all phenomena such as the afflictions (*kleśa*) are simply the *tathatā* (suchness) arising in accordance with conditions, as explained in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*. That text extensively discusses the meaning of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) and "following conditions.
Furthermore, when the sutra says, "All phenomena are identical to *tathatā*," it refers to the *Guanzizai pusa jing* (Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Sutra), the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and others.

The *Sūtra on the Original Radiance* states: "Only Suchness alone remains. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Suchness of ordinary beings is the same as the Suchness of the grasses and trees;
it is the same even for Maitreya. Since all phenomena are suchness, afflictions are likewise so.

Therefore, afflictions are themselves bodhi, and karmic fetters are themselves liberation. Thus, the following section concludes by distinguishing between the provisional and the real to instruct the students.
The second section clarifies the eighteen gates concerning the "entrusting" of delusions (*moha*).

The commentary states: The general purport of this chapter is merely to manifest the shallowness and depth of the stages (*bhūmi*) by means of the coarseness and subtlety of the entrusting of delusions;

it comprehensively incorporates the various distinct discussions found in the sūtras and śāstras, and differs entirely from the previous [section] which was based on the actual severance [of delusions] by specific individuals. Students [should understand this].
One must know that it is improper to insist on a forced interpretation that results in contradiction; this principle is not found in other schools.
This same explanation applies to the *Yi ji er zhang* (The Two Obstructions) and other treatises as well.
The commentary states: The initial heading refers to the division below that reveals the meaning;

according to the text of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) from the Liang dynasty, the intent of this section merely uses the severance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) to illustrate the contemplation prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), and uses the severance of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) to illustrate the realization-contemplation of the stages.
As for the mention of the two hindrances of delusion and wisdom, these are precisely the afflictive and cognitive hindrances, which can be understood by referring to the text.
"Second, [the afflictions of] the mind are severed by relying on the *samāpatti* of the hide, etc.
The commentary explains: First, the dharma and the metaphor are presented; second, the scriptural passage is cited to establish the proof.

That is to say, by relying on the dharma and the metaphor of the three delusions, the shallow and deep stages of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and their three positions are revealed. This means that during the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, from the three stages of the *śaikṣa* (Three Virtuous Stages) up to the first *bhūmi*, [the afflictions] are coarse.
The first two asaṃkhyeya-kalpas are like skin because they are subtle from the second bhūmi to the eighth;

the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa is like flesh because it is even more subtle from the eighth bhūmi until the end of the stages; and that which is like the heart is called "affliction" (kleśa) because, in its general characteristic, it is characterized by agitation.
Third, regarding "by means of these three delusions, up to the mind of emergence, the mind of removal, and so forth":

the commentary explains that because it is difficult to discern the relative superiority or inferiority of the three minds within each stage (*bhūmi*), these three afflictions are used as a metaphor to reveal them.

According to the text of the *Liang She* (The Compendium of the Liang Dynasty), the "thirty-three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*" refers to the subsequent opening of the *Samyaksaṃbuddha* (Equal Enlightenment) stage, making ten in total.
Since there are three minds for each of the stages (*bhūmi*), there are thirty-three [minds] in total.
Fourth, regarding the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) reaching from the supramundane stages up to the Buddha stage:
the commentary states that the headings indicate the positions according to the text, which can be understood accordingly.
Fifth, [the section] "by means of a defiled mind, one reaches this ālayavijñāna.

The commentary explains: first, the statement of the meaning; second, the citation of the text; third, the explanation. Regarding the distinction between coarse and subtle defiled minds, these refer to the six, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses respectively.

Their "residing in three stages" refers to the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi-gata*), and the stage after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-citta*) to manifest them.

Regarding the three bodies—the transformation, reward, and dharma bodies: at the stage prior to the [ten] grounds, by exhausting the functioning of the sixth consciousness (the sense-consciousnesses) in relation to phenomena, one attains the manifestation of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) in its three distinct types.
At the stages from the first ground upward, by exhausting the functioning of the seventh consciousness (the *manas*), one attains the manifestation of the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Here, what is called "response" (*ying*) is precisely the reward body; thus, the character for "response" is pronounced with a level tone (*píngshēng*). Therefore, Paramārtha names it the "reward body."
This is because the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) corresponds with the dharma-body (dharmakāya); alternatively, it is simply called "response" because it accords with the ten stages (bhūmi).

When the stages are exhausted—referring to the exhaustion of the ālayavijñāna and the eight consciousnesses—one attains the manifestation of the dharma-body by remaining far removed from subtle conceptualization.
The remainder is explained according to the text.
The six [purities] are based upon the three obstacles and extend to the manifestation of the Dharmakāya.
The commentary states: because the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) obscures Bodhi, its purification manifests the Saṃbhogakāya;

because the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) obscures liberation, its purification manifests the Nirmāṇakāya; and because the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) obscures the Dharmakāya, its purification is able to manifest it.
Seventh, because one practices to purify [the mind] by means of delusion regarding the three natures up to the attainment of suchness.

The commentary explains: first, the presentation of the meaning; second, the citation of the sūtra; third, the detailed explanation. Within the citation of the sūtra: "All ordinary beings" and so forth indicates the object of delusion;

"What is it? and so forth poses the question and enumerates the categories; "In this way" and so forth demonstrates awakening, which consists of three parts: (1) returning, (2) following, and (3) speech.
That which is the characteristic of accomplishment is the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature), because it is perfectly accomplished; the rest is explained according to the text.
Eighth, from the four obstacles up to the retribution of a Cakravartin King.

The commentary states: By means of the four obstacles manifested through the binding afflictions (*anuśaya*), the distinctions between the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), the three levels of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*), the four stages, the four practices (*catur-caryā*), the four causes (*catur-hetu*), and the four retributions (*catur-vipāka*) are revealed.

All these involve the cessation of obstacles to manifest the stages; based on the stages, practices are established; based on practices, causes are formed; and based on causes, retributions are induced.
This refers to the fact that the nature of the obstacles and the nature of the stages are diametrically opposed, as are the relationship between practices and causes, and causes and [retributions].

When virtue reaches the point of ultimate compliance and goodness is perfected, there are only four types of retributive fruits; these are merely manifest distinctions in the superiority or inferiority of the Universal Monarchs (Cakravartin) who entrust themselves to the task of gathering and transforming beings.
Furthermore, because one has overturned the aforementioned four obstacles, one is called a "Son of the Buddha" (Buddhaputra).
The commentary states: First, the title is presented; below, the four meanings are explained and established.

Regarding the statement that "the seed is like the father" because it transmits the essence through continuity, and "Prajñā is the mother" because she provides the structural support for its completion, [it means that] from the first bhūmi upward, one belongs to the family of the Buddhas.
Thus, one succeeds and upholds the lineage of the Buddhas as a true son, and is not merely an ordinary outsider.
This is that person.
Furthermore, these four kinds [of practice] should be understood as corresponding to the four meanings.
The commentary states: furthermore, these four kinds of integration refer to the mutual correspondence of the four practices; thus, compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem.
Because its function is able to transport one from birth-and-death to Bodhi, it is said to be like a wheel;
because it can transport and turn one toward the place of liberation, it is like the wheel of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*).

One should contemplate how the four items used to describe the carriage—its location, the noble king, the wheel, and the driver—are correlated with the four practices, thereby collectively establishing the meaning of "movement. Reflect upon this.
The second [point] concerns the four obstacles leading to the attainment of the eternal Dharma-body, wherein there is no birth or death.

The commentary states: This refers to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), in which one eliminates residual habits (*vāsanā*) upon reaching the stages above the ground (*bhūmi*) to manifest the distinctions of the four positions. Specifically, in the first three grounds, one extinguishes the habit of *icchantika* (those lacking the aspiration for enlightenment);

by relying on the mundane meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) that accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the purity of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) constitutes the merit of the retribution-body, whereby the [karmic] retribution is extinguished.
The causes and conditions still undergo transformation and change; in the second, fourth, fifth, sixth, and eighth stages, the heterodox and incorrect wisdoms are extinguished.

By taking refuge in what is similar to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), one establishes the roots of virtue; these virtues manifest without fixed location, driving away and benefiting all beings through rewards that eliminate spatial limitations, thereby causing the extinction of the three, seven, eight, and nine stages.
By taking refuge in what is similar to the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), one eliminates the habitual tendencies of fear associated with the two vehicles.

Compliance and protection are collectively designated as samādhi; it is established as the manifestation of virtue because it is not constrained by the eight sufferings and eliminates the subtlest of the subtle within birth and death.
Thus, from the forty stages up to the Buddha-stage, one returns to cessation.

Having abandoned the habitual tendencies of the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), the fruit is fulfilled and the cause is perfected. All things are ultimately firm and solid, constituting right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Concentration is [the state of] stability.
The perfected manifestation of virtue is quiescent and unmoving; because there are no remaining afflictions to be requited, it is said that "there is no birth-and-death.
Because the four virtues are perfected, this extends to what is taught in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises.

The commentary states: "The first interpretation [addresses] the fourth [point], 'birth-and-death'; here, the preceding and following passages refer to the sūtras and śāstras upon which they are based."
Furthermore, among these four, "even reaching" (*zhì yì*) is also a sincere proof.

The commentary explains that this distinguishes the sequence of delusions; from "the fundamental afflictions" (*zhèngshǐ*) downward, it generally distinguishes the eight stages, thereby proving the meaning of the two delusions of the Zhōngjiào (Middle Teaching) regarding the actual severance of afflictions as applied to persons.
Ninth, because one reaches the supramundane within the tenth stage. The commentary states:
herein, the distinction of the ten stages is revealed by means of the mundane and supramundane aspects of both the active afflictions (*kleśa*) and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
this is merely an illustration based on one portion of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Therefore, in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, [defilements] have already been eliminated up to the preceding stage.
The commentary states: "The active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of the three realms are eliminated in equal measure at this stage, which establishes the first meaning;

that they are all said to be 'subtle' establishes the second meaning, as there remains subtle residual habituation (*vāsanā*). The first meaning refers to the first three stages, while the second meaning refers to the fourth stage.
[The section] "Already Gone.
The *Dilun* commentary states that because [the stages] reach [their respective goals], they are said to be "identical.

The commentary explains that the first part is Vasubandhu’s own explanation of the preceding *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*; the subsequent portion is the Great Master [Xuanzang]’s re-explanation of the treatise’s meaning.
This divides the seeds and habitual tendencies of the two obstacles.
Therefore, one should know that this refers specifically to the ultimate teaching (niṣṭhā-deśanā).

The commentary states: "The proximate [conclusion] ties up this section, while the remote [conclusion] ties up the preceding nine; the phrase 'for the most part' (prāyeṇa) is used because it also applies to the initial teaching (ādikarmika-deśanā)."
"Furthermore, in the ten stages, one practices with the mind toward the afflictions.

The commentary explains: "Regarding the phrase 'furthermore, within the distinct characteristics of the ten stages,' this refers back to the preceding section on the stages (*bhūmi*), which distinguishes between the two positions of the mundane and supramundane.
As for the characteristics of the delusions therein, the original text explains them next as follows:"
The commentary states that [the passage] from "by the third stage" up to [the end] serves to manifest those respective stages.

The explanation says: from the seventh stage and below, one is still subject to the active afflictions (*kleśa-prakaraṇa*); it is only from the eighth stage upward that one discusses the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance.
"Eleventh, because this bodhisattva has reached the second stage of the cultivation of ignorance.
The commentary explains: "Within this stage of the bodhisattva" refers back to the second stage among the supramundane stages.

Within this stage, it is further divided into two sub-stages; from the seventh stage downward, the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) that are associated with the cessation of form and mind are made manifest.
In the stage of effortful non-mastery from the eighth bhūmi upward, one relies upon the extinction of subtle habitual tendencies to manifest mastery over form as effortless. Thus,
the *Mūlamahāyānasaṃparigraha-sūtra* states that this extends until the extinction of ignorance.

The commentary states: "From the seventh stage downward, the two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and their karmic retributions are extinguished without remainder" means that because they are associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*) and have transcended the mundane world, there is no grasping toward results.
"In the eighth stage, the ignorance of the habitual tendency for form (*rūpa-vāsanā-avidyā*) is exhausted" means that there are no manifest signs (*nimitta*).

"In the ninth stage, the ignorance of the habitual tendency for mind (*citta-vāsanā-avidyā*) is eliminated" means that there are no signs of transformation (*parāvṛtti*). "In the tenth stage, the two types of habitual tendencies... [are exhausted].
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the absence of the characteristics of karma.
Because the twelve [links] rely upon the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it is said that they are not seen. The commentary states:

first is the establishment of the thesis, and second is the reliance on the text. Within the establishment of the thesis, the nature of differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is provisionally employed through cessation to reveal [the truth].
The path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) relies upon the cessation of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) to manifest the sequence of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

This is because the text states that on the path of seeing one "attains nothing. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "When, regarding the object of cognition, wisdom attains nothing at all, at that time one abides in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), being free from the marks of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*);
thus, discrimination ceases and there is no attainment. Regarding the statement concerning the path of cultivation:
"Non-perception" refers to the fact that in *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), there is neither attainment nor inconceivability; this is supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*).

Because it abandons the two types of heavy impediments (*dausthulya*), it brings about the realization of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Since one realizes the two unsurpassed fruits through this transformation of the basis, it is said that "one does not perceive."
Thirteen: Based on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, [this section concerns] the distinction between the two stages.

The commentary states: Since the afflictions of conceptualization (*vikalpa-kleśa*) are used to manifest the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), and the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are used to manifest the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and because both stages are thus manifested by means of the coarseness and subtlety of the afflictions, the next question is asked:
How is it known that this reaches the point of non-substantial abandonment?

The commentary states: Since it has been repeatedly stated that the seeds of delusion are addressed in conjunction with the stages and positions, why is it not abandoned? This is the question being raised.
"Is it not the case that the conceptualization of the view of self does not yet constitute entry into the Path of Seeing?

The commentary explains: First, false views are revealed, meaning the conceptualization based on three conditions. As for "like the Buddha" and below, this clarifies the ordinary person of the True Teaching;

"this person" and below, this refers to one who aspires to the Buddha-way. This section relies on the absence of falsity rather than actual realization, employing a rhetorical device of returning the question to clarify the underlying intent regarding delusion.
This demonstrates that it is not a case of actual abandonment by a person. If this were actual abandonment, since there is no longer any error here, why would one not realize entry?
If you say that although there is no [error], one has not yet reached the point of entering the vision [of the truth], [we reply:]...
The commentary states: Furthermore, they calculate that those who are not heterodox do not enter the path of vision (darśanamārga) within this [state] because they possess heterodox seeds;
therefore, this is restated.
Since there are no manifest practices, it is instead revealed by means of their absence.
The commentary states: Since there are no longer any manifest practices, even if one were to calculate [the stages], one should enter the provisions (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*) stages.
Regarding the meaning of "stages" (*avasthā*), since the sense has been inverted below, it is established as a metaphorical manifestation.
Furthermore, they are severed by reaching the two stages of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through spontaneous effort (*anābhoga*).
The commentary explains: because these innate [afflictions] are subtle and difficult to eliminate, their distinctions are manifested by associating them with the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Their true meaning is indicated in the subsequent sutra; as for the manas, since the afflictions of the seven consciousnesses are subtle, they pertain to both the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and cultivation.
It is abandoned by means of its respective stage, as can be known from the fact that it is reached in the *Nirābhāsa-śāstra*. The commentary states:
"The second, the grasping consciousness (*grāhaka-vijñāna*) and so forth" refers to the *manas*, which grasps the eighth [consciousness]; therefore, it is called the "grasping consciousness."

Because the delusions of this consciousness are subtle, they are only completely severed upon reaching the stage of Arhat; furthermore, it may also be understood as referring to the six consciousnesses arising together.

Regarding the statement "the second grasping consciousness" and "if one sees the flesh of the consciousness, afflictions, etc.," this refers to the time when one attains the supramundane path through the sixteen moments of mind—namely, the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*)—during the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) which takes the Truths as its object.

The statement that "at that time, what is exhausted is merely the discriminative [afflictions] (vikalpa-prayoga), while what remains unexhausted is merely the residual [afflictions] of cultivation (bhāvanā)" refers precisely to the innate manas;
thus it is said, "this is the second consciousness," which indicates that its lack of intrinsic nature is explained in the same manner as [the preceding].
Fourteenth, regarding the explanation of the two vehicles turning their minds [from the Lesser Vehicle] through discernment (*vikalpa*).

The commentary states: "Regarding the three conditions to be discerned, they are metaphorically presented to manifest the three stages of the *śaikṣas*—namely, the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*), etc.

One should know that they correspond respectively: the ten stages of practice (*caryā*) exclude false teachers and so forth; the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) exclude false teachings; and [the subsequent stage] excludes false contemplation."
This explanation regarding those who proceed directly summarizes the three stages of the Bodhisattva Path of Worthies;

furthermore, because it is taught here in relation to the guidance and conversion of those of the Two Vehicles who turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna, the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi is described as one of "subduing."
Fifteenth, regarding "simultaneously arising" up to "therefore this statement is made":

The commentary explains that the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] are designated as "simultaneously arising" with respect to their active manifestation (*samudācāra*) to metaphorically indicate that from the seventh stage downward, the observation of the mind has interruptions;

they are designated as "permanently suppressed" and "simultaneously arising" to metaphorically indicate that from the eighth stage upward, there is an uninterrupted continuity of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). These two preceding gates [comprise the whole].
This is further elaborated by distinguishing it from the co-emergent (*sahaja*) within the thirteen [categories], and this is presented here as a provisional manifestation.
Furthermore, the sixteenth [category] is established based on this exposition. The commentary states:

first, this is a provisional manifestation in terms of the afflictions; below, it indicates that this is to be understood according to the distinctions between the mundane, the Hīnayāna, and the Mahāyāna.
Seventeenth, to clarify the point of returning to the manifest, the commentary states:
because one eliminates one obstacle per stage until finally reaching the Buddha-stage, there are eleven;
these correspond precisely to the eleven kinds of *dausthulya* (coarse heaviness) in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
Eighteenth: "To manifest the ultimate knowledge by means of what is provisional.

The commentary states: The preceding section manifested the distinctions between the various stages (*bhūmi*), and thus relied upon the "heavy burdens" (*dausthulya*); this present section manifests the difference between the ultimate and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and thus relies upon the various forms of ignorance.
As cited from the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, these two sections together provide scriptural proof for both gates. Some say this refers to the "Dharma-characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
The Mahāyāna takes these very *dausthulyas* (coarse heavinesses) as the objects to be severed and realized; why, then, are they here instead presented as a provisional manifestation? The answer is:

according to that [Mahāyāna] teaching, they are said to be "severed," whereas here, while retaining the reality [of the *dausthulyas*], they are pointed out as being provisional. This is merely an established convention (*prajñapti*). Why?
Because there are teachings but no person, and because it is a conventional designation (*saṃvṛti*) within the Āgamas.
These various meanings are extensive; they may be understood by referring to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* for further details. The commentary states:
"The first section, based on the gate of teaching, formally concludes [the discussion]. Why? This interrogative phrase serves to investigate and explain the underlying reason.

Its intent is to manifest that the profundity of entering realization is difficult for the ordinary cognitive mind (*vijñāna*) to conceive; if this were not made clear, it would be as if one had reached a dead end. Therefore, this is presented here by way of illustration.
The intention [behind this] is threefold: first, to protect the ten stages; second, to eliminate the mind of pride; and third, to cause the arising of faith.
If one relies on the Sudden Teaching, it reaches up to "and non-interruption. The commentary states:
In this teaching, delusions are fundamentally empty and their nature is fundamentally manifest; they can no longer be deliberated upon in terms of being severed or not.
This cuts through [dualistic] proliferation to state that a single thought-moment is itself non-thought.
This should be understood by consulting the textual evidence from the passage beginning with "The nature of the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-svabhāva*).
The commentary states: because the first Buddha asks about the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and Mañjuśrī immediately responds with the ultimate meaning, seeing is itself the Way.
Cessation is the true goal; thus, the *Buddhāvatamsaka* (The Buddha’s Crown) states: "Cessation is bodhi; it is not obtained from others.
If one follows the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), this extends to the severance of all [afflictions].
The commentary explains: First, it clarifies that the nature of delusion is fundamentally fused, and therefore its essence and suchness cannot be described as being obstructed by anything.

The passage below clarifies that although the aspects of subject and object are distinguished within the division of the meaning of "not-knowing" (*ajñāna*), because the true and the false are also mutually penetrating, it says:
"Those delusions which act as obstacles are likewise so. Therefore, the subsequent section relies on fundamental fusion to realize sudden enlightenment and sever delusions suddenly.
Therefore, this is the meaning found in the "Universal Worthy Chapter" (Samantabhadra-parivarta).
The commentary states that the cited passages provide dual proof for both the perfect obstruction and the perfect removal.
Furthermore, the details regarding the severance of delusions are as extensively explained in the sutra.

The commentary states: Regarding the four meanings used for discernment, although the first three involve the severance of all [afflictions] through a single severance, they are still presented from the perspective of the provisional vehicles (*yāna*);
the fourth, however, is based on the fundamental teaching (*mūla-śāsana*). Therefore, the Dharma is taught in this manner. One should reflect upon this meaning.
Furthermore, the previous discussion regarding the three vehicles here is spoken from the perspective of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
The commentary states: "This is because it completely excludes other doctrinal systems. Because it completely excludes them, dependent origination (yuanqi) becomes the arising of nature (xingqi);
thus, one enters this teaching. If, however, one does not disrupt the sequential arrangement (xingbu), it remains the same as the three vehicles and so forth."
If one summarizes the section on the gates of skillful means up to the gate of severing delusions, the commentary states:
"This fully encompasses the essential tenets of all teachings. Because it fully encompasses them, it enables them all to converge upon a single destination.
This subsequently clarifies the harmonious integration of the fundamental and the derivative, serving as a general conclusion that applies to the remaining cases.
